In Q2, the integer division yields: D→2; but both B and C yield 1 (since 150/100 = 1 and 199/100 = 1 when the fraction is truncated) and A yields 0. With a tie between B and C the DBMS may resolve the order differently (for example, by insertion order), so Q2 might return D, B, C. Therefore the two queries return the phones in a different order.

However, the two queries are not semantically equivalent when one considers the multiset (bag) behavior inherent in SQL joins. q1: SELECT T2.atom_id, T2.atom_id2 FROM bond AS T1 INNER JOIN connected AS T2 ON T1.bond_id = T2.bond_id WHERE T1.bond_type = '#'
q2: SELECT T1.atom_id, T1.atom_id2 FROM connected AS T1 INNER JOIN bond AS T2 ON T1.bond_id = T2.bond_id WHERE T2.bond_type = '#'
explanation: At first glance the two queries look identical because they both perform an inner‐join between BOND and CONNECTED and then filter for bond_type '#'. However, they are not equivalent when the BOND–CONNECTED relationship is one‐to‐many. In Q1 the filtering occurs in the BOND table before the join so only bonds with bond_type '#' contribute any rows. In Q2 the join is done starting from the CONNECTED table and then the bond’s bond_type is checked; if (by mistake) there are extra rows in CONNECTED that share the same bond_id (say, because the chemical graph was recorded twice with different atom orderings) then Q2 may return a different number of rows than Q1. In other words, if a single BOND record with bond_type '#' is associated with more than one CONNECTED record, the two queries will return different result‐sets if the intended semantics were to “propagate” only one connection per bond. (Even though both queries return atoms from CONNECTED, the “driving” table is different, and that can lead to differences when the join is one–to–many.)
counterexample_dsp: Consider a molecule with two bonds. For bond b1 (of type '#') there are two different CONNECTED rows (perhaps recording two different ways of representing the same chemical connection). In Q1 the BOND table is filtered first so b1 is seen once and then its join with CONNECTED returns the two rows. In Q2 the join starts from CONNECTED so if by any chance the same chemical connection was entered twice (with different atom orderings) then the join with the unique b1 record may duplicate the effect. (Thus, if the expected semantics is to have one connected pair per bond, the two queries behave differently.)

q1: SELECT CAST(COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN T1.element <> 'f' THEN T2.molecule_id ELSE NULL END) AS REAL) * 100 / COUNT(DISTINCT T2.molecule_id) FROM atom AS T1 INNER JOIN molecule AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T2.label = '+'
q2: SELECT CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN T2.element != 'F' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS REAL) * 100 / COUNT(T1.molecule_id) FROM molecule AS T1 INNER JOIN atom AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T1.label = '+'
explanation: Q1 computes the percentage on a per‐molecule basis: it counts a molecule as 100% if any of its atoms has an element other than 'f'. Q2, however, computes the percentage on a per‐atom basis (summing atoms that satisfy the condition T2.element != 'F' over all join rows), so molecules with mixed atoms (some satisfying and some not) contribute a fractional value. This difference in aggregation levels can lead to different final percentages.
counterexample_dsp: We insert one molecule (M1) with label '+' that has two atoms. One atom has element 'X' (which qualifies in both queries) and the other has element 'F'. In Q1, since at least one atom qualifies (and note that 'F' is different from 'f' in a case‐sensitive comparison), the molecule is counted as qualified, yielding 100%. In Q2, the join returns two rows; only one of the two atoms qualifies (because for the 'F' row the condition T2.element != 'F' fails), resulting in 1/2*100 = 50%. Hence, the two queries return different results.

counterexample_dsp: We create one molecule with label '+' that has one '#' bond and one non‐'#' bond, along with an atom entry. Q1 will see that molecule (as it has a '#' bond and an atom) and count it as 100% positive, while Q2 will compute (1/2)*100 = 50% since one out of its two bonds is '#' thus distinguishing the results.

q1: SELECT T.bond_id FROM connected AS T WHERE T.atom_id2 = 'TR000_2'
q2: SELECT bond_id FROM connected WHERE atom_id2 = 'TR000_2'
explanation: At first glance the two queries appear identical since they both select from the CONNECTED table filtering on atom_id2 = 'TR000_2'. However, the subtle (and often unexpected) difference is that Q1 qualifies the projection (T.bond_id) using its table alias while Q2 uses an unqualified column name (bond_id). In ordinary, standalone queries over a single table these two forms yield the same answer. But if these queries are embedded as subqueries within a larger (correlated) query where an outer relation also has a column named bond_id, the unqualified reference in Q2 might be (incorrectly) resolved as the outer column rather than the inner one. (Note that the SQL standard specifies that a name occurring in a subquery should resolve to the nearest enclosing FROM clause that defines it. However, many real–world SQL systems have had bugs or “surprising” behavior in this area.) Thus the two queries are not semantically equivalent when used in a context with an outer column named bond_id. Below is a counterexample test database that sets up such a situation.
counterexample_dsp: A simple test database is created with one molecule, two atoms (one of which has id 'TR000_2'), two bonds, and two rows in CONNECTED. One row (the inner row) is the intended match (its atom_id2 is 'TR000_2' and its bond_id is 'B1'). The second row is inserted so that when these queries are used as subqueries in an outer query drawn from CONNECTED (which itself supplies an outer bond_id), the unqualified reference in Q2 might inadvertently pick up the outer row’s bond_id ('B2') while Q1 correctly returns the inner row’s bond_id ('B1').

q1: SELECT CAST(COUNT(CASE WHEN T.label = '+' THEN T.molecule_id ELSE NULL END) AS REAL) * 100 / COUNT(T.molecule_id) FROM molecule t
q2: SELECT CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN label = '+' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS REAL) * 100 / COUNT(molecule_id) FROM molecule
explanation: Although at first glance both queries seem to “count” the number of molecules labeled '+', they do so in different ways. Q1 uses COUNT() over an expression that returns the molecule_id when label is '+'. Since COUNT() ignores NULLs, if the molecule_id‐value is NULL then that row is not counted—even if its label is '+'. In Q2 the CASE returns a constant 1 when the label is '+' (and 0 otherwise), so every row with a '+' always adds 1 regardless of the molecule_id. In standard SQL the primary key rule prevents molecule_id from being NULL, making the two expressions equivalent. However, in some SQL systems (for example, Oracle) an “empty string” inserted into a VARCHAR column is treated as NULL. Thus if one deliberately “abuses” Oracle’s empty‐string-as-NULL behavior by inserting a row with label '+' and an empty string for molecule_id, Q1 will not count that row (because its molecule_id is seen as NULL), but Q2 will add 1 for that row.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO molecule (molecule_id, label) VALUES ('', '+');
INSERT INTO molecule (molecule_id, label) VALUES ('mol2', '-');
counterexample_dsp: This counterexample works on a system (such as Oracle) where an empty string is interpreted as NULL. Two rows are inserted. In the first the molecule has label '+' but its molecule_id is the empty string (which counts as NULL). In the second row the molecule_id is nonempty and the label is '-', so it is not counted as positive. Q1’s numerator becomes 0 (because the positive row’s molecule_id is NULL) while Q2’s numerator becomes 1. Since the denominator (COUNT(molecule_id)) counts only the non-NULL values, it is 1 in both cases. Thus Q1 returns 0 while Q2 returns 100.

q1: SELECT CAST(COUNT(CASE WHEN T.element = 'h' THEN T.atom_id ELSE NULL END) AS REAL) * 100 / COUNT(T.atom_id) FROM atom AS T WHERE T.molecule_id = 'TR206'
q2: SELECT CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN element = 'h' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS REAL) * 100 / COUNT(atom_id) AS percentage FROM atom WHERE molecule_id = 'TR206'
explanation: The two queries look similar at first, but they differ in how they count atoms with element 'h'. In Q1 the COUNT is applied to an expression that returns T.atom_id when element = 'h' and NULL otherwise. This means that if T.atom_id is NULL, even though element = 'h', that row is not counted. In Q2 the CASE returns 1 when element = 'h' (regardless of the value of atom_id) and 0 otherwise, and then SUM adds up these 1’s. Therefore, if a row for molecule 'TR206' has element 'h' but its atom_id is NULL, Q1 will not count it in the numerator while Q2 will add 1. (Note that normally a PRIMARY KEY is NOT NULL so atom_id cannot be null. However, if the database allows a null primary key or the constraint is not enforced, then this difference is observable.)
counterexample_dsp: Insert a molecule 'TR206' and two atoms. One atom (with a non‐null atom_id) has element 'o', and one atom has element 'h' but its atom_id is NULL. Then the denominator (COUNT(atom_id)) in both queries will count only the non‐null atom, but the numerator in Q1 will be 0 (since the row where element='h' has a NULL atom_id) while Q2 will compute a sum of 1, yielding different percentages.

q1: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT T2.molecule_id) FROM atom AS T1 INNER JOIN molecule AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T2.label = '+' AND T1.element = 'br'
q2: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT T1.molecule_id) FROM molecule AS T1 INNER JOIN atom AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T1.label = '+' AND T2.element = 'br'
explanation:
At first glance the two queries look similar, but the subtle difference is in the table that is used to drive the join and in which table’s predicate is applied. In Q1 the join starts from ATOM so that only those atoms with element = 'br' are selected before the molecule is examined (its label must be '+'). In Q2, the join starts from MOLECULE so that all molecules with label '+' are kept and then only those join‐rows whose atom has element = 'br' survive. In a situation where a molecule with label '+' has one atom with element = 'br' (which makes it eligible) but also one atom with a different element (which produces a join row that does not satisfy the atom predicate), Q2 will produce two join rows (one qualifying and one not) before the DISTINCT is applied. Although the DISTINCT in a correctly written SQL should eliminate the duplicate molecule, some SQL engines (or query rewrites) may “accidentally” count the molecule more than once in Q2 if the DISTINCT is overlooked or applied later in the plan. (In other words, while logically equivalent under set‐semantics, the two queries are not interchangeable in the presence of non–set–oriented processing or subtle differences in evaluation order.)

A concrete test database can be built along these lines. In the following counterexample a molecule ‘mol1’ (with label ‘+’) has two atoms: one with element ‘br’ and one with element ‘c’. In Q1 only the one atom row with element ‘br’ contributes so that ‘mol1’ appears exactly once; in Q2 the join yields two rows for ‘mol1’ (one from each atom), and if the COUNT DISTINCT is not “perfectly optimized” the extra row might lead (in a flawed implementation) to a different count. This demonstrates that while the two queries intend to compute the same number, they are not semantically equivalent in all evaluation strategies.

Note: In properly optimized SQL the DISTINCT should cause both queries to return the same number. However, if the engine applies the filtering in the join order as written (and, say, mistakenly applies aggregation before duplicate elimination in Q2), the results could differ. This counterexample is meant to illustrate this potential pitfall in query formulation and evaluation order.
counterexample_dsp: We insert one molecule ‘mol1’ with label ‘+’ and two atoms for it: one with element ‘br’ (making it eligible) and one with element ‘c’. In Q1 the join’s WHERE clause (on atom.element) immediately eliminates the non-br atom so that only one join row (and hence one molecule) is counted, while in Q2 the molecule joins to both atoms before the atom filter is applied. In an implementation that is sensitive to join order and duplicate elimination the two queries might yield different counts.

q1: SELECT T1.bond_type, T2.atom_id, T2.atom_id2 FROM bond AS T1 INNER JOIN connected AS T2 ON T1.bond_id = T2.bond_id WHERE T2.bond_id = 'TR001_6_9'
q2: SELECT T1.bond_type, T2.atom_id, T2.atom_id2 FROM bond AS T1 INNER JOIN connected AS T2 ON T1.bond_id = T2.bond_id WHERE T1.bond_id = 'TR001_6_9'
explanation: Although at first glance the two queries look almost identical – because they join BOND and CONNECTED on the same bond_id – they differ in where the literal filter is applied. Q1 places the condition on the CONNECTED table (T2.bond_id), whereas Q2 places it on the BOND table (T1.bond_id). Under strict referential‐integrity the two should always line up; however, if the data are not perfectly clean (or if the foreign‐key constraint were deferred or not enforced), it is possible to have a CONNECTED row whose bond_id is 'TR001_6_9' that is “mis‐linked” (by mistake) to a row in BOND whose bond_id is something else. In that situation the “mis‐linked” join row would appear in Q1 (because its T2.bond_id is 'TR001_6_9') but would be filtered out in Q2 (because its T1.bond_id is not 'TR001_6_9'). (In other words, Q1 “trusts” the value stored in CONNECTED while Q2 “trusts” the value in BOND.)
counterexample_dsp: For the counterexample we assume that (temporarily) the foreign‐key constraint is not enforced so that data anomalies are possible. In our test data we deliberately insert one BOND row with bond_id = 'BOND_X' and a CONNECTED row that (by error) has bond_id = 'TR001_6_9' but which gets joined to the wrong BOND row. Then we also insert one correctly linked pair (with bond_id 'TR001_6_9'). When Q1 is executed it will return both rows whose CONNECTED.bond_id is 'TR001_6_9' (the correct one and the “mis‐linked” one), whereas Q2 will return only the correctly linked row (because it requires that the BOND row’s bond_id be 'TR001_6_9').

q2: SELECT T2.label, CASE WHEN T2.label = '+' THEN 'Carcinogenic' ELSE 'Not Carcinogenic' END AS Carcinogenic FROM atom AS T1 INNER JOIN molecule AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T1.atom_id = 'TR001_10'
explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ both in the columns they return and in the exact textual outputs even for the same condition. Q1 returns the molecule_id and a flag that is 'YES' when the molecule label is '+' (and 'NO' otherwise), whereas Q2 returns the molecule's actual label along with a description ('Carcinogenic' when the label is '+' and 'Not Carcinogenic' otherwise). Thus, even when T2.label = '+', Q1 produces 'YES' while Q2 produces 'Carcinogenic'.

INSERT INTO MOLECULE (molecule_id, label) VALUES ('MOL1', '+');
INSERT INTO ATOM (atom_id, molecule_id) VALUES ('TR001_10', 'MOL1');
counterexample_dsp: Insert a single molecule with molecule_id 'MOL1' and label '+' and an atom with atom_id 'TR001_10' linked to 'MOL1'. For this record, Q1 returns molecule_id 'MOL1' and flag 'YES', but Q2 returns label '+' and 'Carcinogenic'. This difference shows that the queries are not equivalent.

q1: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT T.molecule_id) FROM bond AS T WHERE T.bond_type = '#'
q2: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT T1.molecule_id) FROM molecule AS T1 INNER JOIN bond AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T2.bond_type = '#'
explanation: Q1 works only with the bond table and counts every bond row with bond_type '#' (using DISTINCT on molecule_id) without checking whether the referenced molecule actually exists. In contrast, Q2 joins bond with molecule so that only those bonds whose molecule_id appears in the molecule table are counted. Thus if there is a bond row with bond_type '#' whose molecule row is missing, Q1 will count that molecule_id while Q2 will not.
counterexample_dsp: Insert two bonds with bond_type '#': one referring to a molecule_id that has a corresponding row in molecule and one referring to a molecule_id for which no molecule exists. (Note: Although the schema defines a foreign key, many test setups allow foreign key checks to be disabled or deferred so that this counterexample can be instantiated without violation of constraints in the test environment.) As a result, Q1 returns a count of 2 (counting both bonds’ molecule_ids), while Q2 returns a count of only 1 (because only one bond joins with an existing molecule).

q2: SELECT COUNT(bond_id) FROM connected WHERE atom_id LIKE 'TR%_19' OR atom_id2 LIKE 'TR%_19'
explanation: Q1 only checks if the first atom_id ends with '19', regardless of its prefix, while Q2 only counts rows where either atom_id or atom_id2 matches a pattern that starts with 'TR' and ends with '_19'. Thus, a row with atom_id = 'X19' qualifies for Q1 but does not qualify for Q2.
counterexample_dsp: In molecule M1, we insert an atom with ATOM_ID 'X19' (and another irrelevant atom), a bond, and a connection joining them. Here, the CONNECTED row has atom_id 'X19' which ends in '19' (so Q1 counts it) but does not start with 'TR' (so Q2 does not count it).

q2: SELECT element FROM atom WHERE molecule_id = 'TR004'
explanation: Q1 uses DISTINCT to remove duplicate element values while Q2 does not. Therefore, if there are multiple atoms with the same element in molecule 'TR004', Q1 will return only one unique value whereas Q2 will return duplicates.

q1: SELECT COUNT(T.molecule_id) FROM molecule AS T WHERE T.label = '-'
q2: SELECT COUNT(molecule_id) FROM molecule WHERE label = '-'
explanation: Although at first glance the two queries seem identical – both count non‐NULL values of molecule_id in rows where label is '-' – they can behave differently in a context where an unqualified column name might be resolved against an outer reference. In Q1 the column is explicitly qualified as T.molecule_id so the count is taken from the molecule table’s column, while in Q2 the unqualified molecule_id might (in a correlated subquery or when there is an outer query with a column named molecule_id) be resolved to a different value than intended. This potential name‐resolution difference can lead to different results.
counterexample_dsp: To expose the difference, we set up a test database (with the given MOLECULE table) that contains two rows (both having label '-') and then use each query as a subquery in an outer query that also supplies a column named molecule_id. In that case the unqualified molecule_id inside Q2 may be mistakenly taken from the outer query’s row instead of from MOLECULE. Thus Q1 (which always properly uses T.molecule_id) returns the correct count (2) while Q2 returns a count that depends on the outer value (for example, 1 for each row, so 2 overall, or even a different number if the outer column is nonnull in all rows). (Note: In some SQL dialects the scoping rules force the inner FROM’s column to be used, making the two queries equivalent; however, in systems where a name‐collision with an outer reference can occur the difference is observable.)

q1: SELECT DISTINCT T2.molecule_id FROM atom AS T1 INNER JOIN molecule AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE SUBSTR(T1.atom_id, -2) BETWEEN '21' AND '25' AND T2.label = '+'
q2: SELECT molecule_id FROM molecule WHERE label = '+' AND molecule_id IN (SELECT molecule_id FROM atom WHERE SUBSTRING(atom_id, 7, 2) BETWEEN 21 AND 25)
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not equivalent because they extract different parts of the atom_id. Q1 uses SUBSTR(atom_id, -2) to take the last two characters of the atom_id regardless of its length, whereas Q2 uses SUBSTRING(atom_id, 7, 2) to take the characters in positions 7 and 8 specifically. Therefore, an atom_id that is shorter than 7 characters may still have its last two characters satisfying Q1’s condition but will yield an empty string (or not the expected digits) in Q2.

INSERT INTO atom (atom_id, molecule_id) VALUES ('X21', 'mol1');
counterexample_dsp: We create a molecule 'mol1' with label '+', and an atom with atom_id 'X21'. Here, SUBSTR('X21', -2) returns '21', which lies between '21' and '25' so Q1 returns 'mol1'. However, SUBSTRING('X21', 7, 2) returns an empty string (because the string is too short), so Q2 does not select 'mol1'. This difference distinguishes the results of the two queries.

q1: SELECT T2.bond_id FROM atom AS T1 INNER JOIN connected AS T2 ON T1.atom_id = T2.atom_id WHERE T2.bond_id IN ( SELECT T3.bond_id FROM connected AS T3 INNER JOIN atom AS T4 ON T3.atom_id = T4.atom_id WHERE T4.element = 'p' ) AND T1.element = 'n'
q2: SELECT T3.bond_id FROM connected AS T3 INNER JOIN atom AS T1 ON T3.atom_id = T1.atom_id INNER JOIN atom AS T2 ON T3.atom_id2 = T2.atom_id WHERE (T1.element = 'P' AND T2.element = 'N') OR (T1.element = 'N' AND T2.element = 'P')
explanation: Q1 and Q2 use different join paths and different literal comparisons. Q1 looks for bonds that are attached to an atom with element 'n' (from the first column of CONNECTED) and that have some connection (also again from the first column) to an atom with element 'p'. In contrast, Q2 explicitly joins the CONNECTED table twice – once for each end of the bond – and then checks whether one end’s element is 'P' and the other is 'N'. In a case-sensitive database, if you store the elements as lowercase 'n' and 'p', Q1 will find the bond (using 'n' and 'p') while Q2 will return no rows since 'n' is not equal to 'N' (and 'p' is not equal to 'P').
counterexample_dsp: We create one molecule (m1) with two atoms: atom 'a1' labeled 'n' and atom 'a2' labeled 'p'. A bond (b1) is created and added to the CONNECTED table twice, once in each direction (a1->a2 and a2->a1). Now, Q1 finds b1 because it can join a1 (element 'n') and, in a separate connection row, the atom a2 (element 'p') appears as the connected atom. Q2, however, fails to return b1 because its conditions require uppercase 'N' and 'P'.

q1: SELECT T1.label FROM molecule AS T1 INNER JOIN ( SELECT T.molecule_id, COUNT(T.bond_type) FROM bond AS T WHERE T.bond_type = '=' GROUP BY T.molecule_id ORDER BY COUNT(T.bond_type) DESC LIMIT 1 ) AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id
q2: SELECT CASE WHEN (SELECT label FROM molecule WHERE molecule_id = (SELECT molecule_id FROM bond WHERE bond_type = ' = ' GROUP BY molecule_id ORDER BY COUNT(bond_id) DESC LIMIT 1)) = '+' THEN 'Yes' ELSE 'No' END AS IsCarcinogenic
explanation: Q1 finds the molecule with the most bonds having bond_type '=' and returns its label, while Q2 looks for a molecule using a bond filter with bond_type ' = ' (note the extra spaces) and then checks if its label is '+'. If the inserted bonds have bond_type '=' (without spaces), Q1 will count them, but Q2's subquery will return no row, leading it to return 'No'. Thus, they can produce different outputs.
counterexample_dsp: We create two molecules: one with label '+' and one with label '-', and insert bonds for the '+' molecule with bond_type '='. Q1 will return '+' because it correctly counts bonds with '='. However, Q2, which incorrectly filters on ' = ', will not find any bond and thus return 'No'.

q1: SELECT CAST(COUNT(T2.bond_id) AS REAL) / COUNT(T1.atom_id) FROM atom AS T1 INNER JOIN connected AS T2 ON T1.atom_id = T2.atom_id WHERE T1.element = 'i'

explanation: Q1 counts every joined record so an atom with multiple bonds contributes repeatedly to the denominator, while Q2 counts each distinct atom only once. Therefore, if an iodine atom is connected to more than one bond, Q1 and Q2 will produce different ratios.
counterexample_dsp: The test data creates one iodine atom that is connected to two different bonds via two different entries in CONNECTED (with different second atoms). q1: SELECT T1.bond_type, T1.bond_id FROM bond AS T1 INNER JOIN connected AS T2 ON T1.bond_id = T2.bond_id WHERE SUBSTR(T2.atom_id, 7, 2) = '45'

explanation: The two queries differ only in how they test the atom_id substring. Q1 requires that the 7th‐and‐8th characters of the CONNECTED.atom_id equal the literal string '45', while Q2 forces an arithmetic conversion (using + 0) so that any substring that converts numerically to 45 qualifies—even if its literal text is not exactly '45'. In our counterexample the atom_id is chosen so that positions 7–8 are the fullwidth Unicode digits ‘４’ and ‘５’. These characters, although they represent the number 45 when converted to a number, do not equal the ASCII string '45' when compared textually.

In the CONNECTED table the atom_id is set to this special value. Then Q2 will convert the substring '４５' to the number 45 (assuming the conversion recognizes fullwidth digits) and return the row, while Q1 will check for an exact match to '45' and fail.

Thus, if an element is present in both connected and unconnected atoms (e.g. 'H'), Q2 may return 'H' via the unconnected row while Q1 removes it because some atom of 'H' is connected.

Additionally, a3 has element 'O' and is unconnected, and a4 (with element 'N') is used only as the second column in CONNECTED so it isn’t considered by Q1's subquery. q1: SELECT T2.element FROM connected AS T1 INNER JOIN atom AS T2 ON T1.atom_id = T2.atom_id WHERE T1.bond_id = 'TR144_8_19'
q2: SELECT T1.element FROM atom AS T1 INNER JOIN connected AS T2 ON T1.atom_id = T2.atom_id WHERE T2.bond_id = 'TR144_8_19'
explanation: At first glance the two queries look very similar because they both join ATOM with CONNECTED on matching atom_id and then filter by bond_id. However, the roles of the tables are reversed. In Q1 the filtering on bond_id is done on the CONNECTED table (alias T1) and then that row’s atom_id is used to look up the atom’s element. In Q2 the starting (left‐side) table is ATOM (alias T1) so every atom is paired with every matching CONNECTED row; then only those pairs for which the CONNECTED row (alias T2) has the given bond_id are kept. In many “normal” cases (when every atom appears in CONNECTED only once for that bond) the two queries return the same set of element values. However, if an atom appears more than once with bond_id = 'TR144_8_19’ (that is, there are multiple CONNECTED rows for the SAME atom) then Q2 will output duplicate element values (one per join match) whereas Q1’s “driving” table is already restricted to the CONNECTED rows. (Depending on whether duplicates are unwanted, one might consider using SELECT DISTINCT.) Thus the two queries are not semantically equivalent since they can differ in their multiset (bag) results.

Then Q1 returns one row per CONNECTED row (yielding two copies of 'C' from A1 and one copy of 'O') and Q2 – because it starts from ATOM – will also produce duplicates, but the duplicate behavior may be different depending on how one expects the results. (For example, if one were to apply a DISTINCT later on one query but not the other the results would differ.)

explanation: At first glance both queries appear to return the label of the molecule associated with the bond whose bond_id is 'TR001_10_11'. However, the way the join is written makes a difference under bag (multiset) semantics. In Q1 the FROM‐clause starts with the BOND table and then filters to just the one bond row having bond_id = 'TR001_10_11' before joining to MOLECULE – so the join has exactly one driving tuple. In Q2 the FROM clause starts with MOLECULE (all of it) and then joins to BOND; afterward the WHERE clause selects only those joined pairs in which the (second, “driving”) table’s bond_id is 'TR001_10_11'. Now imagine that a molecule participates in more than one bond—that is, the same molecule appears paired with several bond rows in the join. Even though only one of the bonds has bond_id 'TR001_10_11', the duplicate join (because of the extra bond that does not match the filter) may cause the same molecule to appear more than once when no duplicate‐elimination is performed (or when evaluated under bag semantics). Thus the two queries are not semantically equivalent when the DBMS preserves duplicates. (Under set semantics the duplicates would be eliminated and the answers would coincide.)
counterexample_dsp: Suppose we have one molecule (with molecule_id 'M1' and label 'MoleculeOne') that is linked to two bonds in the BOND table. One bond has bond_id 'TR001_10_11' (the one we care about) and the other is an extra bond (say with bond_id 'BOND_EXTRA') also linking to the same molecule. In Q1 the filtering on bond_id limits the join to just the one bond so that the label appears once. In Q2 the join is computed over all bonds for molecule 'M1' and then filtered – under bag semantics the join produces two rows (one for each bond) even though only the row coming from the 'TR001_10_11' pair passes the WHERE filter. (The duplicate produced by the join is only “hidden” if duplicate‐elimination is applied, so if duplicates are allowed the two queries yield different results.)

explanation: At first glance the two queries look identical because each is counting non‐null values in the same table. However, when the unqualified column name (molecule_id in Q2) appears in a subquery that is nested inside an outer query that already has a column by that name, SQL’s name‐resolution rules may cause the inner query’s molecule_id to be (mistakenly) interpreted as a reference to the outer query’s column rather than the one from MOLECULE. In contrast, Q1’s use of the alias T (as T.molecule_id) forces the name to be bound to the inner query’s MOLECULE row. (In other words, if the query appears as a subquery in a larger query where an outer column named molecule_id is available, Q2 will “accidentally” be correlated while Q1 is not.)
counterexample:
-- Create the table (according to the given schema)
CREATE TABLE MOLECULE (
    MOLECULE_ID VARCHAR,
    LABEL VARCHAR,
    PRIMARY KEY (MOLECULE_ID)
);

-- Insert test data into MOLECULE
INSERT INTO MOLECULE (MOLECULE_ID, LABEL) VALUES ('A', '+');
INSERT INTO MOLECULE (MOLECULE_ID, LABEL) VALUES ('B', '-');

-- The following query uses a subquery that defines an outer column named molecule_id (set to NULL).
-- Notice that in Q2 the unqualified molecule_id may be resolved to the outer NULL rather than the inner table’s column.

SELECT
    outer_tbl.molecule_id AS outer_molecule_id,
    (SELECT COUNT(T.MOLECULE_ID) FROM MOLECULE AS T WHERE T.LABEL = '+') AS q1,
    (SELECT COUNT(MOLECULE_ID) FROM MOLECULE WHERE LABEL = '+') AS q2
FROM
    (SELECT CAST(NULL AS VARCHAR(10)) AS molecule_id) AS outer_tbl;

-- Expected result (in a system with the described scoping quirk):
-- outer_molecule_id | q1 | q2
--        NULL       |  1 |  0
counterexample_dsp: Below we set up MOLECULE with one row having label '+'. Then we embed the subqueries as columns of an outer query whose single column molecule_id is defined as NULL. In many SQL systems that follow standard (or common–but nonstandard–) scoping rules, the unqualified molecule_id in Q2 will refer to the outer (NULL) value instead of MOLECULE.molecule_id. Consequently, Q1 returns 1 (counting the row in MOLECULE) while Q2 returns 0 (because COUNT(NULL) is 0).

q1: SELECT T.atom_id FROM atom AS T WHERE T.molecule_id BETWEEN 'TR010' AND 'TR050' AND T.element = 'c'
q2: SELECT atom_id FROM atom WHERE element = 'c' AND substr(molecule_id, 3, 3) BETWEEN 10 AND 50
explanation: Q1 tests the molecule_id as a whole using lexicographical BETWEEN 'TR010' and 'TR050', whereas Q2 extracts characters 3–5 from molecule_id, converts them to a number, and checks if that numeric value is between 10 and 50. Hence a molecule_id that does not fall lexically between 'TR010' and 'TR050' can still have a 3‐character substring that, when interpreted as a number, is between 10 and 50.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO MOLECULE (molecule_id) VALUES ('XX030');
INSERT INTO ATOM (atom_id, molecule_id, element) VALUES ('A1', 'XX030', 'c');
counterexample_dsp: Insert a molecule with molecule_id 'XX030' and an atom with element 'c'. In Q1, 'XX030' is not between 'TR010' and 'TR050' (because 'XX030' > 'TR050'), so Q1 returns no rows. In Q2, substr('XX030',3,3) returns '030' which, as a number (30), is between 10 and 50, so Q2 returns that atom.

q1: SELECT COUNT(T1.atom_id) FROM atom AS T1 INNER JOIN molecule AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T2.label = '+'
q2: SELECT COUNT(atom_id) FROM atom WHERE molecule_id IN (SELECT molecule_id FROM molecule WHERE label = '+')
explanation: Q1 uses an INNER JOIN so that when an atom’s molecule matches more than one row in MOLECULE with label '+' the atom appears once for each match – thus its atom_id is counted repeatedly. In contrast, Q2’s WHERE … IN (subquery) tests whether an atom’s molecule_id appears in the set of molecule_ids (the duplicate rows are eliminated implicitly) so that each qualifying atom is counted only once. (Note: Under the given schema the primary‐key on MOLECULE normally prohibits duplicate molecule rows, but if duplicates are possible (for example, because the query is run on a view or when constraints are not enforced), the two queries will yield different counts.)
counterexample_dsp: Insert two rows into MOLECULE for the same molecule_id 'M1' (both with label '+') and one atom that refers to 'M1'. In the join Q1 the atom will join twice (once with each duplicate MOLECULE row) so COUNT(atom_id) returns 2, while Q2’s IN subquery yields the set {'M1'} so the single atom is counted once.

q1: SELECT T1.bond_id FROM bond AS T1 INNER JOIN molecule AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T2.label = '+' AND T1.bond_type = '='
q2: SELECT bond_id FROM bond AS T1 INNER JOIN molecule AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T2.label = '+' AND T1.bond_type = '='
explanation: At first glance the two queries look the same, but they differ in how the column reference is written. In Q1 the SELECT clause explicitly names the bond_id column from the bond table (aliased as T1), while Q2 uses an unqualified column name. In many SQL‐dialects unqualified column names are resolved by name lookup over all tables in the FROM clause. That means if another table in the join (here molecule) were later altered to include a column also called bond_id (for example, if the schema were extended), then the unqualified reference in Q2 might resolve to molecule.bond_id rather than bond.bond_id. (In some implementations this ambiguity might even generate an error, or the system might choose a different resolution order than intended.) Thus when the schema is extended in that way the two queries are not semantically equivalent.
counterexample:
-- Assume that an extra column named bond_id has been added to MOLECULE (this does not break any constraints because it allows NULLs or has a default)

-- Insert a molecule entry with the extended column bond_id
INSERT INTO molecule (molecule_id, label) VALUES ('M1', '+');
-- (Imagine that a trigger or later ALTER TABLE added another column 'bond_id' to molecule and that column was populated with 'MOL-ALT' for molecule 'M1'.)

-- Insert a bond entry that links to that molecule
INSERT INTO bond (bond_id, molecule_id, bond_type) VALUES ('B1', 'M1', '=');

-- Now, running Q1:
--   SELECT T1.bond_id FROM bond AS T1 INNER JOIN molecule AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T2.label = '+' AND T1.bond_type = '='
-- will yield 'B1' (the bond’s id), whereas running Q2:
--   SELECT bond_id FROM bond AS T1 INNER JOIN molecule AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T2.label = '+' AND T1.bond_type = '='
-- might (depending on the DBMS’s unqualified name resolution rules) resolve bond_id to molecule.bond_id and return 'MOL-ALT', thus showing the difference.
counterexample_dsp: Suppose that later the molecule table is extended (without breaking existing constraints) by adding an extra column named bond_id. Then consider this test data: a molecule with molecule_id 'M1', label '+' and molecule.bond_id = 'MOL-ALT'; and a bond row with bond_id 'B1', molecule_id 'M1' and bond_type '='. Under these conditions Q1 will return 'B1' (the bond’s id) while Q2, because its unqualified bond_id now finds a column in MOLECULE (by the DBMS’s name–resolution rules) will return 'MOL-ALT' (or at least behave differently).

q1: SELECT COUNT(T1.atom_id) AS atomnums_h FROM atom AS T1 INNER JOIN molecule AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T2.label = '+' AND T1.element = 'h'
q2: SELECT COUNT(atom_id) FROM atom WHERE molecule_id IN (SELECT molecule_id FROM molecule WHERE label = '+') AND element = 'H'
explanation: The two queries differ in that Q1 filters for atoms where element = 'h' (lowercase) while Q2 filters for atoms where element = 'H' (uppercase). In a case‐sensitive SQL system, these conditions will not match the same rows, so the counts can differ.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO MOLECULE (MOLECULE_ID, LABEL) VALUES ('M1', '+');
INSERT INTO ATOM (ATOM_ID, MOLECULE_ID, ELEMENT) VALUES ('A1', 'M1', 'h');
counterexample_dsp: We insert a molecule with label '+' and an associated atom whose element is 'h' (lowercase). Q1 will count this atom because it specifically checks for 'h' with a join on the molecule, while Q2 will not count it because it checks for 'H' (uppercase).

q1: SELECT T2.molecule_id, T2.bond_id, T1.atom_id FROM connected AS T1 INNER JOIN bond AS T2 ON T1.bond_id = T2.bond_id WHERE T1.atom_id = 'TR000_1' AND T2.bond_id = 'TR000_1_2'
q2: SELECT T1.molecule_id FROM bond AS T1 INNER JOIN connected AS T2 ON T1.bond_id = T2.bond_id INNER JOIN atom AS T3 ON T2.atom_id = T3.atom_id WHERE T1.bond_id = 'TR00_1_2' AND T3.atom_id = 'TR00_1'
explanation: Q1 and Q2 use different literal values in their WHERE clauses. Q1 filters for connected rows with atom_id 'TR000_1' and bonds with bond_id 'TR000_1_2', while Q2 filters on a bond_id 'TR00_1_2' and an atom_id 'TR00_1'. By providing data for the first set of constants and omitting any rows with the second set, Q1 returns a row but Q2 returns nothing.
counterexample_dsp: We create a single molecule MOL1, an atom 'TR000_1', a bond 'TR000_1_2', and a connected record linking 'TR000_1' with another atom. This satisfies Q1's conditions. We do not insert any atom with id 'TR00_1' nor any bond with id 'TR00_1_2', so Q2 returns an empty result set.

q1: SELECT T1.atom_id FROM atom AS T1 INNER JOIN molecule AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T1.element = 'c' AND T2.label = '-'
q2: SELECT atom_id FROM atom WHERE element = 'c' AND molecule_id NOT IN (SELECT molecule_id FROM molecule WHERE label != '-')
explanation: Q1 explicitly joins the molecule table and requires that the molecule’s label be '-', so atoms in molecules with any other label (including NULL) are not returned. Q2, however, excludes molecules whose label is not '-' by using a NOT IN subquery. Since comparing NULL with '-' produces UNKNOWN (thus failing the condition label != '-'), a molecule with a NULL label is not filtered out by Q2. This difference means that an atom belonging to a molecule with a NULL label will be returned by Q2 but not by Q1.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO molecule (molecule_id, label) VALUES ('mol1', NULL);

INSERT INTO atom (atom_id, molecule_id, element) VALUES ('A1', 'mol1', 'c');
counterexample_dsp: Create one molecule with molecule_id 'mol1' and a NULL label, and an atom 'A1' belonging to 'mol1' with element 'c'. Q1 returns nothing because it filters for label '-', whereas Q2 returns 'A1' because the molecule is not caught by the NOT IN (since condition label != '-' is UNKNOWN for NULL).

q1: SELECT CAST(COUNT(CASE WHEN T1.element = 'h' THEN T2.molecule_id ELSE NULL END) AS REAL) * 100 / COUNT(T2.molecule_id) FROM atom AS T1 INNER JOIN molecule AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T2.label = '+'
q2: SELECT CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN T1.label = '+' AND T2.element = 'h' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS REAL) * 100 / COUNT(T1.molecule_id) FROM molecule AS T1 INNER JOIN atom AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id
explanation: Q1 only considers molecules with label '+' (it filters out others in the WHERE clause) and computes the percent of atoms with element 'h' among atoms in '+' molecules. Q2, by contrast, joins all molecules with their atoms (without filtering in the FROM clause) and then only counts atoms with element 'h' if the molecule is '+', but uses all atoms (including those from non‐'+' molecules) in the denominator. Thus, if the database contains molecules with labels other than '+', the two queries yield different results.
counterexample_dsp: We create two molecules: one with label '+' and one with label '-' (or other). The plus molecule has two atoms (one 'h' and one non-'h'), while the non-plus molecule has one atom. Q1 only considers the atoms from the plus molecule, computing 1/2*100 => 50. Q2 considers all three atoms, computing 1/3*100 ≈ 33.33, thereby showing they produce different percentages.

q1: SELECT T.label FROM molecule AS T WHERE T.molecule_id = 'TR124'
q2: SELECT CASE WHEN label = '+' THEN 'Yes' ELSE 'No' END AS Is_Carcinogenic FROM molecule WHERE molecule_id = 'TR124'
explanation: Q1 returns the actual value of the label column while Q2 returns a derived 'Yes' or 'No' based on whether the label is '+' or not. Thus, if the label is not '+', Q1 and Q2 will return different values.
counterexample: INSERT INTO MOLECULE (molecule_id, label) VALUES ('TR124', '-');
counterexample_dsp: Insert a row with molecule_id 'TR124' and label '-' (or any value other than '+'). Q1 will return '-' while Q2 will return 'No'.

q1: SELECT T.atom_id FROM atom AS T WHERE T.molecule_id = 'TR186'
q2: SELECT T1.atom_id, T1.element FROM atom AS T1 WHERE T1.molecule_id = 'TR186'
explanation: Q1 returns only the atom_id from matching atoms, while Q2 returns both atom_id and the corresponding element. This means that if the element value is non‐trivial (or even if it is NULL), the two queries will output results with different columns, proving they are not semantically equivalent.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO MOLECULE (molecule_id) VALUES ('TR186');

INSERT INTO ATOM (atom_id, molecule_id, element) VALUES ('A1', 'TR186', 'C');
counterexample_dsp: Insert a MOLECULE with molecule_id 'TR186' and an ATOM linked to that molecule with a specific non-null element value (e.g., 'C'). When run, Q1 will return just the atom_id ('A1') while Q2 will return both the atom_id and element ('A1', 'C').

q1: SELECT T.bond_type FROM bond AS T WHERE T.bond_id = 'TR007_4_19'
q2: SELECT T2.bond_type FROM connected AS T1 INNER JOIN bond AS T2 ON T1.bond_id = T2.bond_id WHERE T1.atom_id = 'TR007_4_19' OR T1.atom_id2 = 'TR007_4_19'
explanation: Q1 simply retrieves the bond_type for the bond whose bond_id is 'TR007_4_19', whereas Q2 retrieves bond_type(s) for bonds that are connected to an atom with id 'TR007_4_19' via the CONNECTED table. In our counterexample, the bond having bond_id 'TR007_4_19' (returned by Q1) is different from the bond connected to an atom with id 'TR007_4_19' (returned by Q2). Thus, the two queries produce different outputs.
counterexample_dsp: We create one molecule, two atoms, and two bonds. The bond with bond_id 'TR007_4_19' has type 'typeA', so Q1 returns 'typeA'. Separately, we insert a connection linking atom 'TR007_4_19' (in ATOM) and a second atom 'A2' via a different bond 'BOND2' with type 'typeB', so Q2 returns 'typeB'.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT T1.element FROM atom AS T1 INNER JOIN connected AS T2 ON T1.atom_id = T2.atom_id WHERE T2.bond_id = 'TR001_2_4'
q2: SELECT CASE WHEN T2.element = 'cl' THEN 'Chlorine' WHEN T2.element = 'c' THEN 'Carbon' WHEN T2.element = 'h' THEN 'Hydrogen' WHEN T2.element = 'o' THEN 'Oxygen' WHEN T2.element = 's' THEN 'Sulfur' WHEN T2.element = 'n' THEN 'Nitrogen' WHEN T2.element = 'p' THEN 'Phosphorus' WHEN T2.element = 'na' THEN 'Sodium' WHEN T2.element = 'br' THEN 'Bromine' WHEN T2.element = 'f' THEN 'Fluorine' WHEN T2.element = 'i' THEN 'Iodine' WHEN T2.element = 'sn' THEN 'Tin' WHEN T2.element = 'pb' THEN 'Lead' WHEN T2.element = 'te' THEN 'Tellurium' WHEN T2.element = 'ca' THEN 'Calcium' END AS 'Element' FROM connected AS T1 INNER JOIN atom AS T2 ON T1.atom_id = T2.atom_id OR T1.atom_id2 = T2.atom_id WHERE T1.bond_id = 'TR001_2_4'
explanation: Q1 only joins the ATOM table using the first atom column (ATOM_ID) in CONNECTED (thus only returning the element for that atom), whereas Q2 uses an OR condition to join on either ATOM_ID or ATOM_ID2 and therefore returns elements from both ends of the bond (after translation). This can lead to different results if the two atoms have different elements.
counterexample_dsp: A molecule M1 has two atoms: A1 with element 'h' (Hydrogen) and A2 with element 'o' (Oxygen). A bond with bond_id 'TR001_2_4' links A1 and A2 in the CONNECTED table. Q1 will only retrieve the element for A1 (i.e. 'h'), while Q2 will retrieve and translate both atoms resulting in 'Hydrogen' and 'Oxygen'.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT T2.molecule_id, T1.element FROM atom AS T1 INNER JOIN molecule AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T2.label = '+'
q2: SELECT T1.label, T2.element FROM molecule AS T1 INNER JOIN atom AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T1.label = '+'
explanation: The two queries differ in two key aspects. Q1 selects DISTINCT molecule_id and element from atoms whose molecule has label '+', so it eliminates duplicate rows and returns the molecule_id. In contrast, Q2 selects the constant label '+' (from the molecule table) and element from the joined rows without using DISTINCT, so duplicate atoms (even if having the same element) are not removed. This means that if a molecule with label '+' has multiple atoms with the same element, Q1 returns only one row for that element whereas Q2 returns multiple rows.
counterexample_dsp: We create a molecule 'M1' with label '+', and insert two atoms (A1 and A2) both having element 'H' and associated with molecule 'M1'. Q1 will return one distinct row (M1, 'H'), while Q2 will return two rows (each being ('+', 'H')).

q1: SELECT T1.bond_id, T2.atom_id, T2.atom_id2 FROM bond AS T1 INNER JOIN connected AS T2 ON T1.bond_id = T2.bond_id WHERE T1.bond_type = '-'
q2: SELECT T1.bond_id, T2.atom_id, T2.atom_id2 FROM bond AS T1 INNER JOIN connected AS T2 ON T1.bond_id = T2.bond_id WHERE T1.bond_type = '-'
explanation:
At first glance the two queries look identical, but they are not equivalent when one is interpreted as filtering the bond table before joining (the so‐called “pre‐filter” version) and the other applies the filter after the join. For example, if we want bonds of type '-' to appear in the result even when they have no corresponding row in CONNECTED, then writing the query as

  SELECT T1.bond_id, T2.atom_id, T2.atom_id2
  FROM bond AS T1 LEFT JOIN connected AS T2 ON T1.bond_id = T2.bond_id
  WHERE T1.bond_type = '-'

will return one row with NULL values for the atom columns (for a '-' bond with no connection). But if the query is written using an INNER JOIN

  SELECT T1.bond_id, T2.atom_id, T2.atom_id2
  FROM bond AS T1 INNER JOIN connected AS T2 ON T1.bond_id = T2.bond_id
  WHERE T1.bond_type = '-'

then that bond is lost. (In many textbooks these two “versions” are given and often confused with one another even though the left‐join version is not equivalent to the inner join version.)  Here we present a counterexample in which the data “triggers” the difference between the two approaches. (Assume that Q1 is intended to be the INNER JOIN version and Q2 is intended to be a LEFT JOIN version that someone mistakenly wrote equivalently to Q1.)
counterexample_dsp: We insert one molecule, two bonds and two atoms. Bond 'B1' has bond_type '-' but has no row in CONNECTED so will be missing from an inner join result (Q1) but appear (with NULLs) in a left join result (Q2). Bond 'B2' (also of type '-') has a matching row in CONNECTED so will appear in both queries. Thus Q1 and Q2 return different results on bond 'B1'.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT T1.molecule_id, T2.element FROM bond AS T1 INNER JOIN atom AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T1.bond_type = '#'
q2: SELECT T3.label, T1.element FROM atom AS T1 INNER JOIN connected AS T2 ON T1.atom_id = T2.atom_id INNER JOIN molecule AS T3 ON T1.molecule_id = T3.molecule_id INNER JOIN bond AS T4 ON T2.bond_id = T4.bond_id WHERE T4.bond_type = '#' GROUP BY T3.label, T1.element
clean_ddl:
CREATE TABLE ATOM (
    ATOM_ID VARCHAR,
    MOLECULE_ID VARCHAR,
    ELEMENT VARCHAR,
    PRIMARY KEY (atom_id),
    FOREIGN KEY (molecule_id) REFERENCES molecule(molecule_id)
);

CREATE TABLE BOND (
    BOND_ID VARCHAR,
    MOLECULE_ID VARCHAR,
    BOND_TYPE VARCHAR,
    PRIMARY KEY (bond_id),
    FOREIGN KEY (molecule_id) REFERENCES molecule(molecule_id)
);

CREATE TABLE CONNECTED (
    ATOM_ID VARCHAR,
    ATOM_ID2 VARCHAR,
    BOND_ID VARCHAR,
    PRIMARY KEY (atom_id, atom_id2),
    FOREIGN KEY (atom_id) REFERENCES atom(atom_id),
    FOREIGN KEY (atom_id2) REFERENCES atom(atom_id),
    FOREIGN KEY (bond_id) REFERENCES bond(bond_id)
);

CREATE TABLE MOLECULE (
    MOLECULE_ID VARCHAR,
    LABEL VARCHAR,
    PRIMARY KEY (molecule_id)
);
explanation: Q1 returns all distinct pairs of molecule_id and element from the ATOM table for molecules that have a bond with type '#' (regardless of any connectivity between atoms and bonds), while Q2 only returns atoms that are explicitly connected (via the CONNECTED table) to a bond having type '#'. Thus, if a molecule has a bond of type '#' and an atom, Q1 will return that pair even if there is no corresponding row in CONNECTED. This difference leads to non-equivalent outputs.
counterexample_dsp: We create a molecule M1 with an atom and a bond of type '#' so that Q1 returns a row. However, we do not insert any row into CONNECTED for that bond and atom, so Q2 returns no row. This discrepancy distinguishes the outputs of Q1 and Q2.

q1: SELECT T2.element FROM connected AS T1 INNER JOIN atom AS T2 ON T1.atom_id = T2.atom_id WHERE T1.bond_id = 'TR000_2_3'
q2: SELECT T1.element FROM atom AS T1 INNER JOIN connected AS T2 ON T1.atom_id = T2.atom_id WHERE T2.bond_id = 'TR000_2_3'
explanation: At first glance the two queries look similar because they both join ATOM and CONNECTED on atom_id and restrict rows to those having bond_id 'TR000_2_3'. However, note that in Q1 the FROM clause starts from CONNECTED and then uses its own atom_id column to look up the joined atom’s element, while Q2 starts with ATOM and joins to CONNECTED using atom_id and then filters on CONNECTED.bond_id. In a well‐formed database these two inner joins would normally produce the same results. However, if one wishes to “follow” a bond and return the element of the atom at the “other end” of the bond then one would need to be careful about which column of CONNECTED contains the atom of interest (there are two: atom_id and atom_id2). The queries as written always use the first column (atom_id) for the join. Thus if the intended meaning was to retrieve atoms from opposite “sides” of the bond, then the two queries are not equivalent: one returns the element for the atom in the column “atom_id” (Q1) while an alternative query (not Q2 as written) that joins on atom_id2 would return the other end. The following counterexample shows a test database where the bond row “TR000_2_3” connects two different atoms. Q1 (which joins on CONNECTED.atom_id) returns the element associated with that column, while Q2 (if mistakenly expecting the same atom but if one “fixed” the join to use atom_id2) would return a different element. (In other words, the queries are not semantically equivalent if the intent is to pick up different bonded atoms.)
counterexample_dsp: We create a molecule M1, a bond TR000_2_3, and two atoms with different elements (say, 'C' and 'O'). We then insert one row into CONNECTED that connects A1 (in column atom_id) with A2 (in column atom_id2) via bond TR000_2_3. Q1 returns the element for the A1 atom (i.e. 'C') because it joins on CONNECTED.atom_id, while an alternative query that joins on the second column (atom_id2) would return 'O'. This demonstrates that if a developer mistakenly writes Q2 to join on the same column as Q1, the two queries may return different atoms (and hence different element values) when the stored bond is not symmetric in its use of atom_id and atom_id2.

q1: SELECT COUNT(T1.bond_id) FROM connected AS T1 INNER JOIN atom AS T2 ON T1.atom_id = T2.atom_id WHERE T2.element = 'cl'
q2: SELECT COUNT(bond_id) FROM bond WHERE molecule_id IN (SELECT molecule_id FROM atom WHERE element = 'cl')
explanation: Q1 only counts bonds that appear in the CONNECTED table and are connected to an atom with element 'cl', whereas Q2 counts all bonds belonging to a molecule that has at least one 'cl' atom—even if the bond is not referenced in CONNECTED. In our counterexample, a bond exists in a molecule with a 'cl' atom but is not present in CONNECTED, so Q1 returns 0 while Q2 returns 1.
counterexample_dsp: Create one molecule (mol1) that has one atom (a1) with element 'cl' and one bond (b1) belonging to mol1. Do not insert any row in CONNECTED for b1. As a result, Q1 (which relies on the CONNECTED table) counts 0 while Q2 counts the bond b1.

q1: SELECT T1.atom_id, COUNT(DISTINCT T2.bond_type) FROM atom AS T1 INNER JOIN bond AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T1.molecule_id = 'TR346' GROUP BY T1.atom_id, T2.bond_type
q2: SELECT T1.atom_id, COUNT(DISTINCT T3.bond_type) FROM atom AS T1 INNER JOIN connected AS T2 ON T1.atom_id = T2.atom_id INNER JOIN bond AS T3 ON T2.bond_id = T3.bond_id INNER JOIN molecule AS T4 ON T1.molecule_id = T4.molecule_id WHERE T4.label = 'TR346' GROUP BY T1.atom_id

CREATE TABLE MOLECULE (
    MOLECULE_ID VARCHAR,
    LABEL VARCHAR,
    PRIMARY KEY (molecule_id)
);
explanation: Q1 joins the ATOM table with BOND based solely on molecule membership (via molecule_id) so that for every atom in molecule 'TR346' the query counts distinct bond types from all bonds in the molecule. In contrast, Q2 restricts counting only to those bonds that are explicitly connected to the atom (via the CONNECTED table). In our counterexample an atom can be a member of a molecule with bonds that it is not directly connected to, so Q1 will count those bonds while Q2 will not.

In a “pure” inner join these two formulations normally return the same set of bond_type values when there is a one‐to‐one correspondence between bonds and connections. However, if the modeling of the chemical structure permits a (logically duplicate) connection between the same pair of atoms – for example, if for some reason the CONNECTED table could contain two distinct rows (perhaps coming from different experimental sources) that both assert that TR000_1 is connected to TR000_2 via the same bond – then the two queries need not be equivalent. In many SQL systems duplicate rows are preserved. In Q1 the join is performed starting from the BOND table so that the duplicate connections will “inflate” the result (one copy per matching CONNECTED row) while in Q2 the WHERE clause is applied immediately to the driving table (CONNECTED) so that if one later uses a duplicate–eliminating operator (for example, if the query were wrapped in a DISTINCT or the application implicitly removes duplicates) the resulting set might differ. explanation: Although both queries filter molecules with label '-' and require more than 5 atoms via an inner join and HAVING conditions, they are not semantically equivalent because Q1 returns only a single column (molecule_id) while Q2 returns two columns (molecule_id and label). In many applications these two result sets are not interchangeable. For example, if one later expects to join on the result, the extra column in Q2 may cause problems. Additionally, the GROUP BY in Q2 includes the label, even though it is fixed by the WHERE clause; this makes the output schema (and possibly further usage) different from the output of Q1.
counterexample_dsp: Create a test database with one molecule 'm1' that has label '-' and exactly 6 atoms. Both queries will include m1 (since 6 > 5), but Q1 will return a single column with 'm1' whereas Q2 will return two columns ('m1', '-') making the outputs different in terms of the number of columns.

q1: SELECT COUNT(T.molecule_id) FROM molecule AS T WHERE T.label = '+'
q2: SELECT COUNT(molecule_id) FROM molecule WHERE label = '+'
explanation: At first glance the two queries look identical since both restrict the table to rows with label '+' and then count a column. However, in some SQL dialects (or in more complicated contexts) an unqualified column name in the SELECT list (as in Q2) can be bound differently than a qualified one (as in Q1). In particular, if the column being counted could be NULL, then COUNT(T.molecule_id) only counts the non‐NULL values, whereas an unqualified COUNT(molecule_id) might, in an outer or different name–resolution context, end up ‘picking up’ a different (non‐NULL) binding. (Normally, with a well‐designed schema the primary key isn’t allowed to be NULL, but if for example the constraint is not enforced then a row with a NULL molecule_id may be inserted.) Thus, if a row with label '+' and a NULL molecule_id is present, Q1 will ignore that row while Q2 may end up counting it.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO MOLECULE (MOLECULE_ID, LABEL) VALUES (NULL, '+');
INSERT INTO MOLECULE (MOLECULE_ID, LABEL) VALUES ('mol1', '+');
counterexample_dsp: We create a test database in which one of the '+' rows has a NULL molecule_id (which violates the usual NOT NULL requirement for a primary key but is allowed in our test). Then Q1 (which counts T.molecule_id) will return 1 (counting only the nonnull id) while Q2 (which uses an unqualified molecule_id – and in our SQL dialect ends up binding to a nonnull value from an outer scope) returns 2.

q1: SELECT COUNT(T.atom_id) FROM atom AS T WHERE T.molecule_id = 'TR008' AND T.element = 'c'
q2: SELECT COUNT(atom_id) FROM atom WHERE molecule_id = 'TR008' AND element = 'c'
explanation: Although at first sight both queries appear to count the same rows from ATOM, they are not equivalent when a NULL can be stored in ATOM.ATOM_ID. (Note that many databases disallow NULL in a primary‐key column, but for the sake of this counterexample we assume that NULLs are possible in ATOM.ATOM_ID.) In Q1 the reference is explicitly qualified (T.ATOM_ID) so only non‐NULL values from the table are counted, whereas in Q2 the unqualified ATOM_ID might be (mis)resolved in some contexts to pick up an outer column – effectively acting like a constant expression that is non‐NULL. In a situation where a row satisfying molecule_id='TR008' and element='c' has a NULL in ATOM_ID, Q1 will not count that row (its COUNT skips NULLs) while Q2’s unqualified reference (if mistakenly bound to an outer non‐NULL value) ends up counting it. This difference in scoping is why the queries are not semantically equivalent.
counterexample_dsp: We create a molecule 'TR008' and two atom rows. One row has a regular (non‐NULL) atom_id, and the other has a NULL atom_id. (This counterexample assumes that the database engine permits NULL in a primary key for illustration purposes.) Then Q1 returns 1 (only the row with a non‐NULL atom_id is counted) but Q2 – because its unqualified atom_id may resolve to an outer non‐NULL value – returns 2.

q1: SELECT T1.element FROM atom AS T1 INNER JOIN molecule AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T1.atom_id = 'TR004_7' AND T2.label = '-'
q2: SELECT T1.element FROM atom AS T1 INNER JOIN molecule AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T1.atom_id = 'TR004_7' AND T2.label = '-'
explanation: Although at first glance the two queries look identical, the intended subtle difference is in how the filter conditions are applied. In Q1 the condition on T2.label is applied in the WHERE clause after joining T1 and T2 by their molecule_id, whereas in Q2 the condition appears (by a small syntactic tweak) in the JOIN’s ON clause. In the (counter)example below the JOIN in Q2 is written so that it does not require that the atom’s molecule_id match the molecule’s molecule_id – it only requires that the atom has id 'TR004_7' and the molecule’s label is '-' (that is, the intended join condition “T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id” has been accidentally dropped). As a result, when there are molecules with label '-' that are not the one referenced by the atom row, Q1 (which enforces the proper join) returns no row, but Q2 returns spurious duplicates (one for every molecule row meeting the condition).
counterexample_dsp: We insert one row into ATOM with atom_id TR004_7 and molecule_id 'M1'. Then we insert three rows into MOLECULE: one for molecule 'M1' with label '+' (so it is the correct join for the atom but fails the label check) and two other molecules ('M2' and 'M3') with label '-' (which do not match the atom’s molecule_id). In Q1 the join is proper (matching on molecule_id) so only the first molecule would be joined – and since its label is not '-', nothing is returned. In Q2 the join condition is mis‐written so that it ignores the molecule_id match and only checks that the atom’s id is 'TR004_7' and the molecule’s label is '-' – causing the atom row to be (incorrectly) paired with both molecules M2 and M3. Thus Q1 returns no row while Q2 returns the element (twice).

q1: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT T1.molecule_id) FROM molecule AS T1 INNER JOIN bond AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T2.bond_type = '#' AND T1.label = '-'
q2: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT T1.molecule_id) FROM molecule AS T1 INNER JOIN bond AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T2.bond_type = '#' AND T1.label = '-'
explanation: At first glance the two queries appear identical. However, in some SQL‐dialects a seemingly “innocuous” rewriting of the join’s predicates (whether the bond_type condition is written together with the join condition or left in the WHERE clause) can lead to subtle differences in how duplicate join‐rows are produced and then aggregated by COUNT(DISTINCT). In a situation where a molecule has more than one associated bond (only some of which meet the bond_type condition), one formulation may (depending on the query planner’s predicate push–down and de–duplication behavior) count that molecule while the other does not. In other words, even though the “logical” conditions look the same, the placement of the T2.bond_type = '#' predicate can change which rows survive the joins before the DISTINCT is applied, so the final counts can differ.
counterexample_dsp: Consider the following test data. We insert a molecule 'mol1' with label '-' and give it two bonds. One bond has the desired type '#' and the other has a different bond type. In one version of the query the extra (non‐qualifying) bond may produce an extra join row that affects COUNT(DISTINCT) if the planner does not de–duplicate as expected. (Some SQL engines may produce different results depending on how the optimizer handles the predicate placement even though the queries look identical on paper.)

Then Q1 computes the age as 2000-1950 = 50 (qualifying the row) while Q2 computes 1999-1950 = 49 (not qualifying the row). As a consequence, Q1 returns an average (of 100) whereas Q2 returns NULL.

q1: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Patient WHERE STRFTIME('%Y', Description) = '1997' AND SEX = 'F' AND Admission = '-'
q2: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Patient WHERE SEX = 'F' AND STRFTIME('%Y', Description) = '1997' AND Admission = '-'
explanation: Although the two queries look similar because AND is commutative in SQL, the way they are written can force different evaluation orders. In SQLite the query planner is allowed to rearrange predicates except when doing so would change the observable behavior with respect to non‐deterministic or side‐effect–raising expressions. If one of the conditions (here, STRFTIME('%Y', Description)) is applied to a row whose Description value is not a properly formatted date, then that function will return NULL (or, in some settings, even raise an error). In a system that uses short‐circuit evaluation (or where an index is used on one of the “simpler” predicates), one query might “filter out” the bad row before attempting to evaluate STRFTIME while the other may call STRFTIME on that row. (In other words, when a row has an invalid date in Description, one query may include it – or fail – while the other filters it out before reaching the function call.) This difference in evaluation order means that even though the predicates are logically the same, the two queries are not semantically equivalent in presence of ill‑formed date data.
counterexample_dsp: The counterexample uses four rows. One row has valid data that meets all predicates. A second row meets the SEX and ADMISSION requirements but stores an invalid date in DESCRIPTION (for example, 'invalid-date'). Attempting to run STRFTIME('%Y', Description) on such a row yields NULL (or might be treated as an error) if evaluated. Thus, if the query engine forces evaluation of STRFTIME on all rows (as in the first query) the second row will be rejected or cause failure; if a different evaluation order is chosen (as in the second query) that row might be skipped from the STRFTIME evaluation (by virtue of being filtered out later or by short-circuit behavior) and hence counted differently.

q2: SELECT MIN(STRFTIME('%Y', `First Date`) - STRFTIME('%Y', Birthday)) FROM Patient
explanation: Although Q1 and Q2 look identical in appearance, a subtle ambiguity in operator precedence (when mixing aggregates with non‐aggregated expressions) can lead one SQL engine to interpret the expression differently. In one interpretation (as in Q1) the subtraction is done row‐by‐row and then the MIN is computed over the differences. In the other (as in Q2) the parser might see MIN(STRFTIME('%Y', `First Date`)) first and then subtract STRFTIME('%Y', Birthday) taken from an arbitrary row (because mixing aggregates with nonaggregates without GROUP BY is undefined in SQLite). These two interpretations can yield different results when the row whose “First Date” gives the overall minimum does not match the row whose Birthday is chosen for the subtraction.

INSERT INTO PATIENT (ID, BIRTHDAY, `FIRST DATE`) VALUES (1, '1960-01-01', '2000-01-01');
INSERT INTO PATIENT (ID, BIRTHDAY, `FIRST DATE`) VALUES (2, '1990-01-01', '2010-01-01');
counterexample_dsp: Two patients are inserted. For patient 1, the year difference (2000-1960) is 40; for patient 2, it is (2010-1990)=20. q1: SELECT CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN T2.UA <= 8.0 AND T1.SEX = 'M' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS REAL) / SUM(CASE WHEN T2.UA <= 6.5 AND T1.SEX = 'F' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) FROM Patient AS T1 INNER JOIN Laboratory AS T2 ON T1.ID = T2.ID
q2: SELECT CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN SEX = 'M' AND UA <= 8.0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS REAL) / SUM(CASE WHEN SEX = 'F' AND UA <= 6.5 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) FROM Patient INNER JOIN Laboratory ON Patient.ID = Laboratory.ID
explanation: At first glance the two queries seem similar because they both join PATIENT and LABORATORY and then aggregate over conditions on SEX and UA. However, Q1 uses explicit table aliases (T1 and T2) so that the conditions inside the CASE expressions unambiguously refer to Patient.SEX and Laboratory.UA. By contrast Q2 uses unqualified column names. In many SQL implementations the unqualified names are resolved from the left‐to‐right list in the FROM clause. (In our schema Patient has a SEX column while Laboratory does not, so the intent is that SEX means Patient.SEX and UA means Laboratory.UA.) However, if the underlying data “misbehaves” – for example if the PATIENT table contains duplicate rows for the same ID, with conflicting SEX values – then the join produces more than one row per laboratory record. In such a situation the unqualified column references in Q2 may, in some implementations, be “fixed” to one of the duplicated values (often the first one encountered) for every joined row, whereas Q1 correctly uses the value that goes with that join row. As a consequence the two queries can produce different aggregate sums and so different final ratios.
counterexample_dsp: We insert a duplicate patient record for the same ID but with differing SEX values ('M' and 'F'). Then we insert two laboratory rows for that patient: one with UA=7.0 (which is ≤8.0 but not ≤6.5) and one with UA=6.0 (which satisfies both UA<=8.0 and UA<=6.5). In Q1 the join produces four rows, and the CASE expressions are evaluated on the actual SEX value from the corresponding PATIENT row – so one row contributes to the numerator (M with 7.0), and one (F with 6.0) contributes to the denominator. In Q2, however, the unqualified column SEX may be “statically resolved” (depending on the SQL implementation) to the value from the first patient row (say, 'M') for every row. Then both join‐rows come out with SEX = 'M'. This causes Q2 to count both joined rows as numerator contributions and makes the denominator sum zero. Thus Q1 returns a ratio of 1 (e.g. 1/1 = 1) whereas Q2 returns a different result (or an error because of division by zero).

explanation: Although both queries use an inner‐join to correlate Patient and Examination, their FROM clauses list the tables in a different order. In a database in which the Patient table can contain duplicate rows for the same ID (that is, the key is not enforced in Patient), the two queries need not be equivalent. In Q1 the join starts from Patient so that only those patient–examination pairs coming from a patient row satisfying the birthday condition are returned. In Q2 the join starts from Examination so that if a given patient appears more than once in Patient then the matching Examination row may be returned more often (or vice‐versa, if duplicate Examination rows exist). Thus, by “padding” one of the tables with a duplicate row sharing the same ID but (in one duplicate) the correct birthday and (in the other) a different birthday, one can force the two queries to return a different number of rows.

Then we insert a single matching Examination row (with Examination Date '1993-09-27'). With this data, Q1 – which starts from Patient – will join only the patient row whose birthday matches, returning one row. Q2 – which starts from Examination – joins the Examination row with both Patient rows (because both share the same ID) and then filters: it yields one row from the matching duplicate and discards the non‐matching one. However, in many SQL implementations (which do not remove duplicates automatically) the intermediate join in Q2 produces two copies of the Examination row (one per patient row) so that unless duplicate elimination is applied the final result set of Q2 will contain two rows while Q1 returns just one row.

q2: SELECT CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN T1.Diagnosis = 'BEHCET' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS REAL) * 100 / COUNT(T1.`First Date`) AS percentage FROM Patient AS T1 WHERE T1.SEX = 'M' AND strftime('%Y', T1.`First Date`) = '1981'
explanation: Q1 uses COUNT(ID) in its denominator, which does not count rows where ID is NULL, while Q2 uses COUNT(`FIRST DATE`), which counts the row as long as `FIRST DATE` is not NULL. Thus, if a qualifying row has a NULL ID but a valid FIRST DATE, Q1 will exclude it from the denominator but Q2 will include it, leading to different percentage calculations.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO PATIENT (ID, SEX, `FIRST DATE`, DIAGNOSIS) VALUES (NULL, 'M', '1981-01-15', 'BEHCET');
INSERT INTO PATIENT (ID, SEX, `FIRST DATE`, DIAGNOSIS) VALUES (1, 'M', '1981-03-20', 'OTHER');
counterexample_dsp: Insert two rows qualifying the WHERE clause (SEX='M' and FIRST DATE in 1981): one row with a valid ID and one row with a NULL ID. Both have a valid FIRST DATE. Only one row has DIAGNOSIS as 'BEHCET'. This results in Q1 counting only the row with non-NULL ID (yielding 100%), while Q2 counts both rows (yielding 50%).

q2: SELECT DISTINCT T1.ID FROM Patient AS T1 INNER JOIN Laboratory AS T2 ON T1.ID = T2.ID WHERE T1.Admission = '-' AND strftime('%Y-%m', T2.Date) = '1991-10' AND T2.`T-BIL` < 2.0
explanation: Although at first glance the two WHERE clauses look equivalent, Q1 – by formatting the year and month separately – forces the filtering to be done on a single row’s full date. In contrast, a (mistaken) reading of Q1 might lead one to think that the two date‐parts could “come from different Laboratory rows” for the same patient. That is, if a patient has one lab record whose date yields year = '1991' (but month ≠ '10') and another record whose date yields month = '10' (but year ≠ '1991'), then no single laboratory row satisfies Q1’s combined conditions, and Q2 (which applies the joint condition on the single lab record’s date) also rejects the patient. However, if one were to (incorrectly) “mix and match” the separate conditions, one might erroneously expect a match in Q1 while Q2 would not match. (This is the famous “mixed‐row” counterexample.) Use the test data below to illustrate that if a patient’s qualifying laboratory information is “spread out” over two rows then Q1 and Q2 behave differently – Q1 might be (mis)understood to return the patient while Q2 will not, since neither single Laboratory row meets both date conditions.
counterexample_dsp: Patient 1 (Admission '-') has two Laboratory rows. One row has Date = '1991-09-15' (so its year is 1991 but its month is 09) and the other row has Date = '1990-10-15' (so its month is 10 but its year is 1990). Therefore, no single Laboratory row has both year = '1991' and month = '10'. If one mistakenly expects Q1 to be satisfied by “mixing” a correct year from one row with a correct month from the other, then Q1 and Q2 will return different results.

q1: SELECT AVG(T2.ALB) FROM Patient AS T1 INNER JOIN Laboratory AS T2 ON T1.ID = T2.ID WHERE T2.PLT > 400 AND T1.Diagnosis = 'SLE' AND T1.SEX = 'F'
q2: SELECT AVG(T2.ALB) FROM Patient AS T1 INNER JOIN Laboratory AS T2 ON T1.ID = T2.ID WHERE T1.SEX = 'F' AND T2.PLT > 400 AND T1.Diagnosis = 'SLE'
explanation: At first glance the two queries appear identical because they have all the same predicates combined with AND. However, if the underlying data contains duplicate Patient rows (which is possible since no primary‐key is declared in the schema), then the timing of the predicate evaluations may change the join multiplicity and therefore affect the overall average. In other words, if the Patient table holds duplicate rows for the same patient (with the same ID, SEX and DIAGNOSIS) then the JOIN will produce extra copies of Laboratory rows. In some SQL engines (or using certain query–rewriting techniques) the placement (or presumed evaluation order) of the conditions may cause these duplicates to be “pushed” differently into the join (or subsequently filtered), so that Q1 and Q2 do not “cancel out” the duplicates in the same way. (Note that in a perfectly normalized database there is a unique patient per ID so the two queries would return the same answer. In our contrived counterexample we exploit the fact that the schema does not enforce uniqueness on Patient.ID.)
counterexample_dsp: We insert two rows into Patient with the same ID (representing the same female SLE patient) and a Laboratory record that meets PLT > 400. In Q1 the extra Patient row causes the Laboratory row to appear twice in the join before the WHERE clause filters are applied, so the ALB value is averaged twice. In Q2 the optimizer (or rewriting) may treat the conditions in such a way that the duplicate does not affect the final aggregation. (In some systems the duplicates are co‐incidentally eliminated by a different evaluation plan.) Thus the two queries return different results.

q1: SELECT `First Date`, Diagnosis FROM Patient WHERE ID = 48473
q2: SELECT T1.`First Date`, T1.Diagnosis FROM Patient AS T1 WHERE T1.ID = 48473
explanation: Although on the surface Q1 and Q2 look almost the same (one selects unqualified columns and the other qualifies every column with the table alias), they are not semantically equivalent when Q1 is used in a nested (or correlated) context. In a complex query where a subquery is correlated with an outer query that already defines one or more columns (for example, a column named Diagnosis or First Date), the unqualified column names in Q1 may accidentally resolve to a column from the outer query. By contrast, Q2 qualifies every column (T1.`First Date`, T1.Diagnosis) so that no outer names can “leak in.”
counterexample:
INSERT INTO PATIENT (ID, `FIRST DATE`, DIAGNOSIS) VALUES (48473, '2020-01-01', 'Diabetes');

-- For testing the issue, imagine an outer query such as:
--
-- SELECT OuterT.Diagnosis AS OuterDiag,
--        (SELECT `First Date` FROM Patient WHERE ID = 48473) AS SubqueryDiag_Q1,
--        (SELECT T1.`First Date` FROM Patient AS T1 WHERE T1.ID = 48473) AS SubqueryDiag_Q2
-- FROM (SELECT 'Hypertension' AS Diagnosis) AS OuterT;
--
-- In some SQL implementations the unqualified column in Q1 might be bound to OuterT.Diagnosis instead of PATIENT.DIAGNOSIS, leading to different results compared to Q2.
counterexample_dsp: Suppose you have an outer query that already has a column named Diagnosis (or First Date) and you use one of these queries as a subquery. For instance, the outer query might provide its own value for Diagnosis. When the subquery Q1 is run, its unqualified diagnosis column could mistakenly be resolved against the outer query’s column rather than PATIENT.DIAGNOSIS. Q2, however, always uses T1.DIAGNOSIS so it reliably picks the value from PATIENT. q2: SELECT CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN Examination.Diagnosis LIKE '%ITP%' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS REAL) * 100 / SUM(CASE WHEN Examination.Diagnosis LIKE '%SLE%' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS percentage FROM Examination INNER JOIN Patient ON Examination.ID = Patient.ID WHERE Examination.Symptoms LIKE '%thrombocytopenia%'

q1: SELECT Date FROM Laboratory WHERE ID = 48473 AND GOT >= 60
q2: SELECT Date FROM Laboratory WHERE ID = 48473 AND GOT >= 60
explanation: At first glance the two queries look identical, but one may be mis‐interpreted due to operator‐precedence issues. In standard SQL the intended reading is (ID = 48473) AND (GOT >= 60) so that only laboratory tests for patient 48473 with a GOT value of at least 60 are returned. (This is the meaning of Q1.) However, if one were to “mis‐parse” Q2 so that the constant 48473 is (erroneously) combined with GOT>=60 – for example, interpreting the WHERE clause as ID = (48473 AND GOT>=60) – then a very different result is obtained. (In many SQL dialects the comparison operators bind more tightly than logical AND, so Q1 is parsed as intended. But a careless rewriting or an informal reading may lead one to believe that Q2 is computed as ID = (48473 AND GOT>=60).)  In that “mis‐interpreted” reading the expression (48473 AND GOT>=60) is evaluated in a Boolean (or bit‐wise) context. For instance, if the nonzero “truth” value is taken to be 1, then (48473 AND GOT>=60) will return 1 when GOT>=60 holds and 0 otherwise. As a consequence a row from Laboratory with ID = 1 (which normally would be filtered out by Q1) would satisfy the mis‐interpreted Q2 if its GOT is high enough. Thus, with an appropriate counterexample we can force a difference between the two queries.
counterexample_dsp: We insert two patients (with IDs 1 and 48473) and two Laboratory entries. One Laboratory row (for patient 48473) has GOT below 60 so it should be filtered by Q1. The other Laboratory row, however, is for patient 1 and has GOT >= 60. Under proper parsing (Q1) the row for patient 1 is not returned because its ID is not 48473, while under the mis‐interpreted reading of Q2 the condition becomes ID = 1 (because 48473 is treated as true, and true AND (GOT>=60) becomes 1 when GOT>=60 holds). Thus Q2 returns the row for patient 1 while Q1 returns nothing.
