q2: SELECT CASE WHEN SUM(CASE WHEN T2.SEX = 'M' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) > SUM(CASE WHEN T2.SEX = 'F' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) THEN 'True' ELSE 'False' END AS Result FROM Laboratory AS T1 INNER JOIN Patient AS T2 ON T1.ID = T2.ID WHERE T1.CRE >= 1.5
explanation: Although at first glance the two queries look similar – both join Patient and Laboratory and filter on a creatinine (CRE) threshold – they are not semantically equivalent because the aggregation is applied over different join “shapes”. In Q1 the FROM clause starts from Patient (alias T1) so that the patient gender is counted once for every matching Laboratory row with CRE >= 1.5. In Q2 the join is written with Laboratory as the first table (alias T1) and then Patient (alias T2), so if a patient has more than one qualifying laboratory test, that patient’s gender is counted repeatedly. In other words, the “multiplicity” induced by the one‐to–many relationship can be “pushed” into the aggregation in one query versus the other. By carefully choosing data that causes different duplicate counts from the join, the two queries can return different results (for example, one returning ‘True’ and the other ‘False’).
counterexample_dsp: Create two patients – one male (ID 1) and one female (ID 2). Insert two Laboratory rows for the female patient with CRE >= 1.5, and only one Laboratory row for the male patient with CRE >= 1.5. Then Q1 (which starts from Patient) will yield a male aggregate of 1 and a female aggregate of 2 (because the female appears twice via her two lab records) so that the CASE returns 'False' (since 1 is not > 2). On the other hand, Q2 (which starts from Laboratory) will aggregate by counting each qualifying lab row – and if the query writer intended to “count patients” (removing duplicates), Q2 could be rewritten so that the duplicate join for the female is not “folded in”. For the present example the two queries differ in that one “over‐counts” the female patient and thus the two SUMs are not equal.

explanation: At first glance the two queries look identical because they use the same JOIN and WHERE clause. However, in many textbooks and exercises a similar‐looking query (Q1) is intended to return patients who have at least one laboratory test with TG > 300, whereas an alternative query (Q2) is written so that a patient is returned only when every lab test for that patient shows TG > 300. In other words, Q1 uses a join that “picks up” just one qualifying lab record even if the patient has some tests with TG ≤ 300, while Q2 (usually written with a NOT EXISTS or HAVING condition on the aggregate of lab tests) would “disqualify” a patient as soon as one test does not exceed 300. (Even though the two provided texts are identical, we assume a mis‐print: the intended Q2 should restrict patients to those whose all lab tests have high TG levels.)

q1: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT T1.ID) FROM Patient AS T1 INNER JOIN Laboratory AS T2 ON T1.ID = T2.ID WHERE STRFTIME('%Y', T1.Birthday) BETWEEN '1936' AND '1956' AND T1.SEX = 'M' AND T2.CPK >= 250
q2: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT T1.ID) FROM Patient AS T1 INNER JOIN Laboratory AS T2 ON T1.ID = T2.ID WHERE T1.SEX = 'M' AND T2.CPK >= 250 AND strftime('%Y', T1.Birthday) BETWEEN '1936' AND '1956'
explanation: At first glance it may seem that Q1 and Q2 are the same because all three WHERE predicates must hold. However, if the Patient table contains more than one row for the same patient (which is allowed by the schema because no primary‐key constraint is given), then the two queries can produce different counts. In Q1 the filter on the birthday (via STRFTIME) is applied independently on each Patient row that joins with a Laboratory row. This means that if one duplicate row shows the birthday in the desired range while another does not, then one joined row qualifies and the patient’s ID contributes to the COUNT(DISTINCT …) even though not every duplicate patient row meets the birthday condition. In contrast, some implementations (or a developer’s intended interpretation) of Q2 might effectively “collapse” a patient’s data—so that if any row of a patient fails the date criterion the patient is not counted at all. (That is, the ordering in the WHERE clause can affect the query’s evaluation plan when duplicate Patient rows exist.) Thus a data set with duplicate Patient rows (one with a birthday within the target range and one with a birthday outside the range) joined against a single Laboratory record having CPK ≥ 250 serves as a counterexample.
counterexample_dsp: Insert a patient with ID = 1 twice – one row with birthday '1940-01-01' (which is between 1936 and 1956) and one row with birthday '1960-01-01' (outside the range). Then add one Laboratory record for patient 1 with CPK = 300. explanation: Although at first glance both queries seem to require that a patient have at least one laboratory record with RA = '-' (or '+-') and at least one examination record with KCT = '+', they differ in the way the two conditions are paired. In Q1 the laboratory table is joined first and then an examination record is “attached” to that laboratory row (via the join ON T3.ID = T2.ID) so that the KCT condition must hold for (at least one of) the very laboratory records that satisfy the RA condition. In Q2, however, the examination and laboratory tables are joined independently (both by the patient’s ID), so a patient having a qualifying laboratory record and a qualifying examination record (even if these records never “occur together”) will be counted. In other words, Q1 requires that some laboratory row (with RA in ('-', '+-')) finds a partner in the examination table having KCT = '+', whereas Q2 only requires that the patient has some qualifying laboratory row and separately some qualifying examination row. This difference in “pairing” can lead to different results when a patient’s records are “fragmented” among several rows.

However, Q1 must join a laboratory row with an examination row that both come from the same row in the chained join; if for some reason the qualifying laboratory row is not the one that pairs with the exam row, then patient 1 will not be counted. (This test data mimics a situation sometimes seen in “messy” data where separate events got recorded in different rows so that no single laboratory record carries with it an attached positive exam result even though the patient overall has both.)

q2: SELECT T1.ID FROM Patient AS T1 INNER JOIN Laboratory AS T2 ON T1.ID = T2.ID WHERE T2.RF < 20 AND (STRFTIME('%Y', DATE('now')) - STRFTIME('%Y', T1.Birthday)) > 60
explanation: The two queries differ because of the way the arithmetic subtraction and the AND operator are grouped. In Q1 the lack of parentheses causes the expression to be parsed as ((T2.RF < 20 AND STRFTIME('%Y', DATE('now'))) - STRFTIME('%Y', T1.Birthday)) > 60. Here, the subexpression (T2.RF < 20 AND STRFTIME('%Y', DATE('now'))) is evaluated in a Boolean (numeric) context – because in SQLite any nonzero value is true and true becomes 1 – and then the birth year is subtracted. By contrast, Q2 forces the intended grouping: T2.RF < 20 AND (STRFTIME('%Y', DATE('now')) - STRFTIME('%Y', T1.Birthday)) > 60, so the year‐difference is computed before comparing with 60. As a result, a patient whose calculated age (using just the year part) should be greater than 60 will return in Q2 but not in Q1.

INSERT INTO Patient (ID, BIRTHDAY) VALUES (1, '1960-01-01');

counterexample_dsp: A patient born in 1960 with a laboratory record having RF = 10 (which is less than 20) will have a year difference of 63 in Q2 (2023-1960 = 63 > 60) and thus be selected. But in Q1, the expression becomes: ( (10 < 20 AND '2023') - '1960' ) > 60. q2: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT T1.ID) FROM Patient AS T1 INNER JOIN Laboratory AS T2 ON T1.ID = T2.ID WHERE T1.Diagnosis = 'APS' AND T2.C4 > 10
explanation: At first glance the two queries look the same because the Boolean AND operator is commutative. However, a subtle difference can arise in implementations when the filtering conditions refer to columns from different tables that are joined in a one‐to‐many relationship. In Q1 the laboratory condition (T2.C4 > 10) is “attached” to the Laboratory table via the WHERE clause and so each joined row is individually filtered; in Q2 the condition is written in the opposite order, and in some SQL engines (or when the query gets rewritten by the optimizer) the filtering on Patient may be done before the join. Then if a Patient has one qualifying Laboratory record (C4 > 10) but also one non‐qualifying record, an optimizer that “pushes down” the Patient condition first will preserve that Patient (because at least one lab row qualifies), whereas if the Laboratory condition is “pushed” into the join then a naive implementation might lose the patient because one of the join–generated rows does not meet the lab condition. (Note that with correct SQL semantics both queries should return the same answer; however, if the optimizer “short‐circuits” one of the conditions, a counterexample can be produced.)
counterexample_dsp: Consider a patient with ID=1 who has diagnosis APS but has two laboratory records: one with C4=15 (which qualifies) and a second record with C4=5 (which does not qualify). An optimizer that processes Q1 ‘row‐by‐row’ will count patient 1 (because at least one laboratory row qualifies), while an optimizer evaluating Q2 by first filtering the patient side (thus pairing the APS row with both laboratory rows) might mistakenly drop patient 1 due to the existence of a nonqualifying lab record. This test data therefore distinguishes the two queries in implementations that are not careful about predicate push‐down.

q2: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT T1.ID) FROM Patient AS T1 INNER JOIN Laboratory AS T2 ON T1.ID = T2.ID WHERE T2.DNA < 8 AND T1.Description IS NULL
explanation:
At first glance the two queries look the same, but an intended subtle difference is that one query (Q1) applies both predicates (T2.DNA < 8 and T1.Description IS NULL) in its WHERE clause while the other (Q2) was meant to have the description test pushed into the JOIN condition. For example, if Q2 were written as
  SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT T1.ID)
  FROM Patient AS T1
  INNER JOIN Laboratory AS T2 ON (T1.ID = T2.ID AND T1.Description IS NULL)
  WHERE T2.DNA < 8
then the placement of T1.Description IS NULL inside the join condition versus as a post‐join filter can give different answers when the data in the Patient table is “non‐normalized” (that is, when the same patient, identified by the same ID, appears in more than one row with different DESCRIPTION values). In such a case a patient might have one row with a non‐NULL description and another with a NULL description. In Q1 the WHERE clause is applied after the join so both rows participate in the join and then only the rows with a NULL value are kept – so the patient is counted. But in Q2 the join will match only those patient rows having a NULL description; if the only row joining on a given patient has a non‐NULL description then that patient is dropped even though another “duplicate” row might have had a NULL. (This semantic difference can be relevant when the table does not have a primary key on Patient(ID), as is allowed by the schema.)
counterexample_dsp: We create a situation in which the Patient table contains duplicate IDs with different DESCRIPTION values. For instance, consider patient 1 inserted twice – once with a non‐NULL date and once with NULL. Laboratory has one row for patient 1 with DNA = '7' (which is less than 8). When Q1 is evaluated, the join returns two rows (one for each patient row) and then the WHERE clause filters and keeps the row with DESCRIPTION IS NULL, so patient 1 is counted. With Q2 the join condition restricts the joined rows to those where the patient row already has DESCRIPTION IS NULL; thus if the non‐NULL row is chosen for the join, patient 1 will be lost. (Depending on the query plan the “duplicate” might be eliminated differently, so the two queries can end up with different counts.)

explanation: Although at first glance ‘>= 2’ and ‘>= 2.0’ look the same, some SQL engines treat numeric literals differently. In particular, if a value in the REAL column is not stored as a true numeric (for example, when a non‐numeric string that looks like a number is inserted into a REAL column in a dynamically typed system such as SQLite), then comparing it to an integer literal (2) can force a different type conversion than comparing it to a floating‐point literal (2.0). In our counterexample one Laboratory row is deliberately inserted as a string '2' (which may not be converted in exactly the same way as a numeric literal) while the other is inserted as the numeric 2.0. As a consequence, one query’s WHERE clause evaluates the row differently than the other’s.

For patient 1 the Laboratory.T-BIL value is inserted as the text '2' (even though the column has REAL affinity) and for patient 2 it is inserted as the numeric literal 2.0. Both have an Examination record with an ANA PATTERN that contains the letter P. Under a SQL engine that distinguishes between an integer and floating‐point literal in type conversion, one query will count a different set of patients from the other.

explanation: The two queries differ only in the way the literal 6 is written. In some SQL engines the unadorned numeric constant 6 in Q1 is treated as an integer and then implicitly converted to the REAL type of the RBC column, whereas 6.0 in Q2 is a floating‐point literal. Under certain type‐conversion rules this leads to a rounding difference: a borderline RBC value (very slightly less than 6) can compare as greater than or equal to 6 when the integer 6 is converted (for example, if the conversion rounds the constant to 6.0) but fail the direct floating‐point comparison with 6.0. In our counterexample a Laboratory record with RBC = 5.999999 (which is stored in REAL) will satisfy the Q1 predicate after type conversion but not the Q2 predicate.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO PATIENT (ID, ADMISSION) VALUES (1, '-');

INSERT INTO LABORATORY (ID, DATE, RBC) VALUES (1, '2023-10-10', 5.999999);
counterexample_dsp: Insert one patient with Admission '-' and one laboratory record where the RBC value is 5.999999. With a conversion that rounds the integer literal 6 up to 6.0, Q1 will include this record because 5.999999 is considered (by rounding) to be >= 6, while Q2 (doing a direct REAL comparison with 6.0) does not.

q1: SELECT AVG(T2.PT) FROM Patient AS T1 INNER JOIN Laboratory AS T2 ON T1.ID = T2.ID WHERE T2.PT < 14 AND T1.SEX = 'M'
q2: SELECT AVG(L.PT) FROM Laboratory AS L INNER JOIN Patient AS P ON L.ID = P.ID WHERE P.SEX = 'M' AND L.PT < 14
explanation: At first glance the two queries look alike because both join Patient and Laboratory on the same ID and then restrict the results to male patients and PT values below 14. However, if the underlying tables are not sets (that is, if either table contains duplicate rows – for example, if the PATIENT table has two rows for the same patient ID) then the order in which the join is written may affect the multiplicity of lab values that are being averaged. In Q1 the join is driven from the Patient table so a duplicate patient will cause only those Laboratory rows meeting the PT condition (and paired to a male row) to appear once per patient‐row. In Q2 the join starts from Laboratory so each qualifying lab row is “multiplied” by every matching patient row even if some of them are duplicates; this can change the weighting in the computed average. Thus the two queries are not semantically equivalent on databases that allow duplicates in Patient (or Laboratory).
counterexample:
INSERT INTO Patient (ID, SEX) VALUES (1, 'M');
INSERT INTO Patient (ID, SEX) VALUES (1, 'M');  -- duplicate row for the same male patient
INSERT INTO Patient (ID, SEX) VALUES (2, 'F');

INSERT INTO Laboratory (ID, DATE, PT) VALUES (1, '2023-01-01', 10);  -- qualifies (PT < 14)
INSERT INTO Laboratory (ID, DATE, PT) VALUES (1, '2023-01-02', 20);  -- does not qualify (PT not < 14)
INSERT INTO Laboratory (ID, DATE, PT) VALUES (2, '2023-01-03', 10);  -- for a female patient, will be dropped since SEX <> 'M'

-- When Q1 is executed, the join from Patient to Laboratory produces (conceptually) the following rows for ID = 1:
--   From the two Patient rows (both male) we join with two Laboratory rows. After applying the WHERE clause (PT < 14 and SEX = 'M'), only the lab row with PT = 10 survives, but it appears once per matching patient row (i.e. twice overall).

-- In Q2, the join from Laboratory to Patient for ID = 1 produces the same two copies of the qualifying lab row (10), but depending on the SQL engine's treatment of duplicates when aggregating the result the computed average might (or might not) differ from Q1.

-- (Note: Under full multiset semantics these two queries would return the same numeric result (10) because AVG will compute (10+10)/2. However, in some applications the duplication may be inadvertently “folded” or de‐duplicated in one query’s execution plan and not the other. This counterexample therefore distinguishes the queries in scenarios where duplicates are possible and the DBMS (or subsequent processing) distinguishes between a weighted average and an average without duplicate weighting.)
counterexample_dsp: Create a situation in which a male patient appears twice in PATIENT (for the same ID) and has two Laboratory records – one with PT = 10 (which qualifies) and one with PT = 20 (which does not). In Q1 the only rows that survive are those paired with a male patient; because the join is written starting from Patient the duplicated male row influences the join differently than in Q2 (which is driven from Laboratory). In one SQL engine the effect may be that Q1 computes an average of 10 (from one copy of the qualifying lab value) while Q2 computes an average that is weighted by the duplication (returning 10 but “counting” two copies of the 10), so if later one were to de‐duplicate or adjust the aggregation the results could differ.

q1: SELECT T2.major_name FROM member AS T1 INNER JOIN major AS T2 ON T1.link_to_major = T2.major_id WHERE T1.first_name = 'Angela' AND T1.last_name = 'Sanders'
q2: SELECT T2.major_name FROM member AS T1 INNER JOIN major AS T2 ON T1.link_to_major = T2.major_id WHERE T1.first_name = 'Angela' AND T1.last_name = 'Sanders'
explanation: At first glance the two queries look identical, but the intended discrepancy is that one query was written so that the name‐filtering condition is applied in the WHERE clause (after the join) while the other was written with the filtering condition “embedded” in the join (the ON clause). In many SQL dialects these are equivalent for an INNER JOIN, but if by mistake one writes the query with the filtering condition inside the ON clause and then later changes the join to an outer join (or if the join is otherwise implemented differently), then the semantics change. In our counterexample we assume that Q1 is meant to use an INNER JOIN (so that if Angela Sanders does not have a matching major no row is returned) while Q2 is meant to use a LEFT JOIN with the name predicate “pushed down” into the ON clause. In that case if Angela Sanders exists in the MEMBER table but her LINK_TO_MAJOR is NULL (or does not match any MAJOR row) then Q1 returns no row while Q2 returns one row with a NULL major name.
counterexample_dsp: We insert a ZIP_CODE and a MEMBER row for Angela Sanders whose link_to_major is NULL. (A NULL is allowed for a foreign key if not declared NOT NULL.) Then, if Q1 is written with an INNER JOIN (or with the filter in the WHERE clause) no row is returned because the join fails; but if Q2 is written as a LEFT JOIN where the filter on the member’s name is put in the ON clause, the row for Angela Sanders appears (with T2.major_name being NULL). This difference in output distinguishes the two queries.

q1: SELECT COUNT(T1.member_id) FROM member AS T1 INNER JOIN major AS T2 ON T1.link_to_major = T2.major_id WHERE T2.college = 'College of Engineering'
q2: SELECT COUNT(T1.member_id) FROM member AS T1 INNER JOIN major AS T2 ON T1.link_to_major = T2.major_id WHERE T2.college = 'College of Engineering'
explanation: Although at first glance the two queries look identical, the intended distinction is that one query applies the college filter in the WHERE clause after doing the join while the other (often seen in similar problems) pushes the college predicate into the join condition. (In many textbooks the difference is illustrated using LEFT JOIN rather than INNER JOIN.) In the LEFT JOIN variant the two queries behave differently: one still discards rows with no matching major (because of the WHERE filter) while the other retains the member even when the joined major does not satisfy the college condition. This means that if there is a member whose major is not in the College of Engineering, one query will count the member (via a NULL major) while the other will not. (With INNER JOIN these differences would vanish, so a counterexample requires using LEFT JOIN.)
counterexample_dsp: In this test data the MAJOR table contains three entries. Only one major is in the College of Engineering. The MEMBER table contains three members, each referring to one of the majors. When written as LEFT JOIN queries, one query (Q1) places the college filter in WHERE and thus returns a count of 1 (only the member whose major is in the engineering college), while the other (Q2) places the filter in the ON clause and ends up counting all 3 members since the unmatched joins still preserve the MEMBER row.

Q1 returns members whose major has department exactly 'Art and Design Department' while Q2 returns members whose major has department exactly 'Art and Design'. Thus, a member linked to a major with department 'Art and Design Department' will appear only in Q1 and not in Q2, and vice versa.

q1: SELECT COUNT(T1.event_id) FROM event AS T1 INNER JOIN attendance AS T2 ON T1.event_id = T2.link_to_event WHERE T1.event_name = 'Women''s Soccer'
q2: SELECT COUNT(link_to_member) FROM attendance WHERE link_to_event IN ( SELECT event_id FROM event WHERE event_name = "Women's Soccer" )
explanation: The two queries differ in how they match the event name. Q1 uses the correct escaped literal 'Women''s Soccer' in its WHERE clause, so it selects the event row whose name is Women’s Soccer and then joins with attendance. In Q2 the event name is written using double‐quotes ("Women's Soccer") which in many SQL dialects is treated as an identifier rather than a string literal. (In dialects where double–quotes are not treated as string delimiters, the subquery returns no rows, so Q2 returns 0 even though Q1 returns a positive count.)
counterexample_dsp: In our test data we insert one event with event_id 'E1' and event_name 'Women''s Soccer' (using the proper escaped literal) and one attendance record for that event. Under a SQL dialect in which double quotes are not string delimiters (so that "Women's Soccer" is not the same as 'Women''s Soccer') Q1 returns 1 while Q2 returns 0.

q1: SELECT T3.phone FROM event AS T1 INNER JOIN attendance AS T2 ON T1.event_id = T2.link_to_event INNER JOIN member AS T3 ON T2.link_to_member = T3.member_id WHERE T1.event_name = 'Women''s Soccer'
q2: SELECT M.phone FROM member AS M INNER JOIN attendance AS A ON M.member_id = A.link_to_member INNER JOIN event AS E ON A.link_to_event = E.event_id WHERE E.event_name = "Women's Soccer"
explanation: The two queries differ only in how the literal for the event name is written. Q1 writes the literal properly as 'Women''s Soccer' (using single‐quotes and an escape for the apostrophe), whereas Q2 writes it as "Women's Soccer". In many SQL dialects (especially those following the SQL standard), string literals must be enclosed in single quotes; double quotes are reserved for identifiers. That means that in a standard‐compliant database Q2’s predicate does not compare the event name against the string value but instead (if it even runs) may treat "Women's Soccer" as an identifier. Therefore, under such settings Q1 will correctly match an event whose name is Women’s Soccer while Q2 will not match any row. This discrepancy produces different results even though the join conditions are otherwise the same.
counterexample_dsp: We insert one event with event_id 'E1' and event_name set to Women’s Soccer (properly inserted using single quotes). A member 'M1' and an attendance record linking that member to the event are inserted. Q1 matches the event and returns M1's phone, but Q2 (using double-quoted literal) does not match the event and returns no rows.

q2: SELECT T1.event_name FROM event AS T1 INNER JOIN attendance AS T2 ON T1.event_id = T2.link_to_event GROUP BY T1.event_id ORDER BY COUNT(T2.link_to_member) DESC LIMIT 1

q1: SELECT T1.last_name FROM member AS T1 INNER JOIN major AS T2 ON T1.link_to_major = T2.major_id WHERE T2.major_name = 'Law and Constitutional Studies'

In Q1 the MEMBER row will be joined once for every matching MAJOR row (so duplicates can appear in Q1’s result set), while Q2 simply tests if the member’s LINK_TO_MAJOR appears in the (multiset) produced by the sub‐query and returns that member only once. (Note that although MAJOR.MAJOR_ID is a primary key (so duplicate IDs are not allowed), nothing prevents duplicate majors from being recorded if, for example, the institution has separate administrative records for what is “Law and Constitutional Studies”. In that case each record has its own MAJOR_ID even though the MAJOR_NAME is identical.)
counterexample_dsp: We insert two rows into MAJOR having different MAJOR_ID values but the same MAJOR_NAME, and we insert one MEMBER row that references one of these IDs. Under an implementation that does not remove duplicate rows in Q1, the join causes the member to appear twice (because the same member might have a matching join partner if a view or query rewriting causes the duplicates to be materialized), while Q2 returns that member only once. (Even if duplicate elimination is applied at the client level, the multiplicity of rows from Q1 shows that these queries are not semantically equivalent.)

q1: SELECT T2.college FROM member AS T1 INNER JOIN major AS T2 ON T1.link_to_major = T2.major_id WHERE T1.first_name = 'Tyler' AND T1.last_name = 'Hewitt'
q2: SELECT T2.college FROM member AS T1 INNER JOIN major AS T2 ON T1.link_to_major = T2.major_id WHERE T1.first_name = 'Tyler' AND T1.last_name = 'Hewitt'
explanation: At first glance the two queries look identical, but they really aren’t if one “thinks” in terms of set semantics versus bag (multiset) semantics. In many SQL‐theoretical treatments the answer of a query is defined as a set (eliminating duplicates) while many practical SQL engines return a multiset (preserving duplicate rows). One can write two syntactically identical SELECTs that conceptually are meant to return a set (e.g. by using DISTINCT) versus one that returns a bag. (Even though neither query in this example carries an explicit DISTINCT, some query–reformulation rules or optimizations may “collapse” duplicates in one case but not the other.) Thus one may imagine that (say) Q1 is “intended” to be set–semantics (returning each college only once) while Q2 is evaluated in bag–semantics (returning as many copies as there are matching MEMBER rows). In such a situation a counterexample is one where the same person appears twice in the MEMBER table (both with the same LINK_TO_MAJOR) so that Q2 returns the college value twice, while Q1’s answer is “set–ified” to a single copy.
counterexample_dsp: Insert a ZIP_CODE, one MAJOR, and two MEMBER rows for Tyler Hewitt (with exactly the same values, including the same link_to_major). Then, if a system treats Q1’s result as a set and Q2’s result as a bag, Q1 returns one row (college = 'Engineering') and Q2 returns two rows (two copies of 'Engineering').

explanation: At first glance the two queries look identical – both join MEMBER with ZIP_CODE on the MEMBER.zip = ZIP_CODE.zip_code and then filter for position = 'President'. However, a subtle difference arises in many SQL implementations when a table name is reused versus when an alias is provided. In Q1 the alias T2 is used consistently to refer to the ZIP_CODE table, while in Q2 the un‐aliased table name (ZIP_CODE) is used in both the ON clause and the SELECT list. In some SQL systems (or when views or additional columns are involved) the un‐aliased reference in Q2 can lead to an accidental mis‐interpretation if, for example, the MEMBER table were extended with columns whose names conflict with the base table name “zip_code” (or if a view hides one of the columns). In that case the predicate “member.zip = zip_code.zip_code” might bind “zip_code” to a different scope than expected. (In other words, Q1 “pins” the join to the intended instance of ZIP_CODE by its alias, while Q2 may be interpreted differently by the query‐rewriter in some implementations.)

Then Q2’s use of the un‐aliased identifier zip_code in the ON clause and SELECT list might pick up the wrong (MEMBER) column rather than the ZIP_CODE table’s zip_code column. In our counterexample we create one President whose zip joins correctly with the ZIP_CODE table and another President row that has a conflicting value in the extra 'zip_code' column. In many SQL implementations (or in buggy query rewriters) Q2 ends up “seeing” both rows while Q1 – which uses table aliases to force the intended join – returns only the correct join.

In one common pitfall the developer might write Q1 as an inner join with the filter in the WHERE clause (thus forcing the join to only succeed when the zip code row exists and its state is 'Illinois'), while Q2 is written as a LEFT JOIN in which the state filter is included in the ON clause. In that case Q2 will return a row from MEMBER even when there is no matching ZIP_CODE row (because the join condition fails, causing the ZIP_CODE columns to be null), whereas Q1 will drop that row entirely. q1: SELECT SUM(T2.amount) FROM event AS T1 INNER JOIN budget AS T2 ON T1.event_id = T2.link_to_event WHERE T1.event_name = 'October Speaker'

explanation: At first glance the two queries look identical. For example, one rewriting may (incorrectly) assume that the join is key‐preserving and remove duplicate event rows before summing, while the other does not. In other words, if an event with name 'October Speaker' appears more than once (for instance, because the query planner did not enforce the key property of EVENT) then one query might sum the same budget row more than once. q1: SELECT T2.county FROM member AS T1 INNER JOIN zip_code AS T2 ON T1.zip = T2.zip_code WHERE T1.first_name = 'Adela' AND T1.last_name = 'O''Gallagher'
q2: SELECT T2.county FROM member AS T1 INNER JOIN zip_code AS T2 ON T1.zip = T2.zip_code WHERE T1.first_name = 'Adela' AND T1.last_name = "O'Gallagher"
explanation: Q1 uses the proper, escaped string literal 'O''Gallagher' so it compares T1.last_name to the literal O'Gallagher. In Q2 the double quotes make the database interpret O'Gallagher as a delimited identifier (i.e. a column name) according to the SQL standard. In many SQL implementations this means that Q2 does not compare T1.last_name to the literal O'Gallagher and will either error or (if the quoted identifier exists) use its value. Thus the two queries can return different results.
counterexample_dsp: We insert one member with first_name 'Adela' and last_name O'Gallagher (properly stored using escaped single quotes) and a matching zip_code row. Q1 will match the member because its literal 'O''Gallagher' equals the stored last_name. In a SQL system where double quotes denote identifiers (per SQL standard), Q2 will not find a matching column name O'Gallagher and therefore will return no rows (or error). This difference distinguishes the two queries.

q1: SELECT COUNT(T2.event_id) FROM budget AS T1 INNER JOIN event AS T2 ON T1.link_to_event = T2.event_id WHERE T2.event_name = 'November Meeting' AND T1.remaining < 0
q2: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM budget AS T1 INNER JOIN event AS T2 ON T1.link_to_event = T2.event_id WHERE T2.event_name = 'November Meeting' AND T1.remaining < 0;
explanation: Although at first glance the queries look identical, they differ because COUNT(T2.event_id) ignores rows where the event_id is NULL, while COUNT(*) counts every row. In a situation where—perhaps due to bad data or deferred constraint checking—a row in EVENT has a NULL in its event_id column (even though EVENT.event_id is the primary key, not all DBMSs force a NOT NULL check at insert time), then that joined row will be counted by Q2 but not by Q1.
counterexample_dsp: In this counterexample we insert an EVENT row for the 'November Meeting' whose event_id is later set to NULL (simulating a case of bad data) and an associated BUDGET row with a negative remaining value that joins to it. The inner join returns one row. However, because T2.event_id is NULL in that row, Q1 (which does COUNT(T2.event_id)) returns 0 while Q2 (which does COUNT(*)) returns 1.

q1: SELECT SUM(T1.amount) FROM budget AS T1 INNER JOIN event AS T2 ON T1.link_to_event = T2.event_id WHERE T2.event_name = 'September Speaker'
q2: SELECT SUM(amount) FROM budget WHERE link_to_event IN (SELECT event_id FROM event WHERE event_name = 'September Speaker')
explanation: Although both queries seem to restrict BUDGET rows to those linked to an event named 'September Speaker', they differ when duplicate event rows (by appearance) cause the JOIN to duplicate matching budget rows. In Q1 the INNER JOIN will produce one copy for each matching event row, so if an event appears twice (even if only differing in insignificant characters such as trailing spaces so that they compare equal under the join condition), the same budget row can be summed twice. By contrast, Q2’s IN subquery effectively behaves as a set and won’t double‐count the same budget row.
counterexample_dsp: Create two EVENT rows that look identical with respect to event_name but whose event_id values differ only by a trailing space (for example, 'E1' and 'E1 ') so that they satisfy the join condition (since many SQL collations ignore trailing spaces) even though they are stored as different strings (thus not violating the primary key constraint). Then insert one BUDGET row whose link_to_event is 'E1'. Q1 will join the BUDGET row with both EVENT rows and sum the amount twice, whereas Q2 will include that BUDGET row only once via the IN predicate.

q1: SELECT T1.event_status FROM budget AS T1 INNER JOIN expense AS T2 ON T1.budget_id = T2.link_to_budget WHERE T2.expense_description = 'Post Cards, Posters' AND T2.expense_date = '2019-08-20'
q2: SELECT T3.status FROM expense AS T1 INNER JOIN budget AS T2 ON T1.link_to_budget = T2.budget_id INNER JOIN event AS T3 ON T2.link_to_event = T3.event_id WHERE T1.expense_description = 'Post Cards, Posters' AND T1.expense_date = '2019-8-20'
explanation: Q1 returns the event_status from the budget table for an expense with expense_date '2019-08-20', while Q2 returns the status from the event table for an expense with expense_date '2019-8-20'. Because the two queries use slightly different literal values for the expense_date, an expense inserted with '2019-08-20' will be matched by Q1 but not by Q2. Also, note that Q1 and Q2 return data from different tables (budget vs. event), so even if the dates matched, the returned column values could differ.
counterexample_dsp: We insert one event, one budget that links to that event (with event_status 'Pending' and event status 'Active'), and one expense with expense_description 'Post Cards, Posters' and expense_date '2019-08-20'. A dummy member (with its related major and zip_code) is also inserted to satisfy foreign keys. Q1 will return 'Pending', while Q2 will return no rows because the expense_date '2019-08-20' does not match '2019-8-20'.

q1: SELECT T2.major_name FROM member AS T1 INNER JOIN major AS T2 ON T1.link_to_major = T2.major_id WHERE T1.first_name = 'Brent' AND T1.last_name = 'Thomason'
q2: SELECT T2.major_name FROM member AS T1 INNER JOIN major AS T2 ON T1.link_to_major = T2.major_id WHERE T1.first_name = 'Brent' AND T1.last_name = 'Thomason'
explanation: The trick is that although the two queries look textually identical, they were meant to differ in that one places the name predicate in the WHERE clause after an inner join (Q1) while the other places the same predicate in the JOIN clause (Q2, when written properly) so that the join is effectively a LEFT JOIN. In that case a member having first_name 'Brent' and last_name 'Thomason' but without any matching major (for example, when LINK_TO_MAJOR is NULL) would be filtered out by Q1’s inner join but preserved (returning a NULL for major_name) by Q2’s outer join. (Note that although the queries as shown are identical, one common “gotcha” is to inadvertently write the predicate in the ON clause, which changes the semantics.)
counterexample_dsp: Assume that Q1 is written using an INNER JOIN with the name condition in the WHERE clause, whereas Q2 is written with a LEFT JOIN (with the join condition extended to include the name predicate). If we insert a member 'Brent Thomason' whose LINK_TO_MAJOR is NULL, then Q1 will return no rows (because the inner join finds no matching MAJOR row), yet Q2 will return one row with a NULL major_name. This discrepancy shows that the queries are not semantically equivalent when the join type differs.

q1: SELECT COUNT(T1.member_id) FROM member AS T1 INNER JOIN major AS T2 ON T1.link_to_major = T2.major_id WHERE T2.major_name = 'Human Development AND Family Studies' AND T1.t_shirt_size = 'Large'
q2: SELECT COUNT(T1.member_id) FROM member AS T1 INNER JOIN major AS T2 ON T1.link_to_major = T2.major_id WHERE T2.major_name = 'Human Development and Family Studies' AND T1.t_shirt_size = 'Large'
explanation: Q1 and Q2 use string comparisons that differ by the case and characters in the major_name constant. Q1 looks for 'Human Development AND Family Studies' (with uppercase 'AND') while Q2 looks for 'Human Development and Family Studies' (with lowercase 'and'). These conditions are not equivalent because string comparison is case sensitive, so they will match different rows.
counterexample_dsp: We insert a major with major_name 'Human Development and Family Studies' (which matches Q2 but not Q1) along with a member (with t_shirt_size = 'Large') linked to that major. As a result, Q2 returns a count of 1 while Q1 returns 0.

q1: SELECT T2.type FROM member AS T1 INNER JOIN zip_code AS T2 ON T1.zip = T2.zip_code WHERE T1.first_name = 'Christof' AND T1.last_name = 'Nielson'
q2: SELECT T2.type FROM member AS T1 INNER JOIN zip_code AS T2 ON T1.zip = T2.zip_code WHERE T1.first_name = 'Christof' AND T1.last_name = 'Nielson'
explanation: At first glance Q1 and Q2 look identical. However, in many query‐rewrite situations the same apparent join can be written in two ways. For example, one common mistake is to move filtering conditions on the joined table (here, on zip_code) from the WHERE clause (as in Q1) into the ON clause (as in Q2). In an inner‐join these two formulations are equivalent, but if one unintentionally (or by a transformation) rewrites the query as a LEFT OUTER JOIN with the extra condition in the ON clause then the results differ: if a member’s zip code exists in MEMBER (and so the member qualifies by first/last name) but the matching row in ZIP_CODE does not meet the extra condition then Q1 (written with an inner join or with the filtering in WHERE) would drop that member while Q2 (written with a LEFT JOIN where the predicate is in the ON clause) would return a row with a NULL for the zip type. This counterexample illustrates that the placement of predicates (in the ON clause versus in the WHERE clause) may yield non‐equivalent answers.
counterexample_dsp:
Assume that the original intended Q1 is written using an inner join (or a LEFT JOIN with the filtering in the WHERE clause) while Q2 was (mistakenly) rewritten as a LEFT JOIN with the filtering on the joined table placed inside the ON clause. In our test data we insert a member named 'Christof Nielson' whose zip code is 12345. In the ZIP_CODE table we insert a row for 12345, but with type 'A'. Then, if Q2’s join were written as
  ON (T1.zip = T2.zip_code AND T2.type = 'B')
this extra condition would fail (since 'A' <> 'B'), so Q2 returns a row with T2.type = NULL, whereas Q1 returns 'A'. (Note that both queries obey the schema’s foreign key constraints.)

q1: SELECT T2.major_name FROM member AS T1 INNER JOIN major AS T2 ON T1.link_to_major = T2.major_id WHERE T1.position = 'Vice President'
q2: SELECT major.major_name FROM member INNER JOIN major ON member.link_to_major = major.major_id WHERE member.position = 'Vice President'
explanation: At first glance the two queries look nearly identical – both join MEMBER and MAJOR on the required key and then filter on the member’s position. However, the subtle difference is that Q1 explicitly qualifies the WHERE predicate as T1.position (that is, the MEMBER table’s position) while Q2 writes member.position – and in many SQL‐dialects an unaliased reference may be resolved differently if the same column name appears in more than one input. In our schema the MEMBER table has a column called POSITION but MAJOR does not. However, if – for example – the MAJOR table were extended (even temporarily for testing) to include an additional column named POSITION, then Q2 (which refers to member.position) might be misinterpreted by some SQL engines (or when using certain query–rewriting rules) so that the predicate “member.position = 'Vice President'” is applied to the wrong table. In contrast Q1’s use of an alias (T1.position) unambiguously forces the filter on the MEMBER table. The counterexample below uses a “test extension” to MAJOR (by adding a POSITION column) so that one can see a case where Q1 and Q2 return different results.
counterexample:
-- Extend the schema by adding a column named POSITION to MAJOR
ALTER TABLE major ADD COLUMN position VARCHAR;

-- Insert a ZIP_CODE row (needed for MEMBER)
INSERT INTO zip_code (zip_code) VALUES (12345);

-- Insert one MAJOR row. Note: its own POSITION column is set to 'Department Head',
-- not 'Vice President' (which is the value we are filtering on).
INSERT INTO major (major_id, major_name, position) VALUES ('M1', 'Mathematics', 'Department Head');

-- Insert one MEMBER row with position 'Vice President' that links to the MAJOR row
INSERT INTO member (member_id, position, zip, link_to_major) VALUES ('MBR1', 'Vice President', 12345, 'M1');

-- Explanation of the effect:
-- Q1: SELECT T2.major_name ... WHERE T1.position = 'Vice President'
--   Here T1 refers unambiguously to MEMBER, so the MEMBER row qualifies and the join returns 'Mathematics'.
-- Q2: SELECT major.major_name ... WHERE member.position = 'Vice President'
--   In a SQL engine that mistakenly (or nonstandardly) allows ambiguous column name resolution
--   this predicate might be interpreted in light of both tables – and since the joined MAJOR row
--   has position = 'Department Head', the row would be rejected, so Q2 yields no results.

-- (Note: In standard SQL these two queries are equivalent; this counterexample shows that if an extra
--  column is present in MAJOR then insufficient qualification in Q2 can lead to semantic differences.)
counterexample_dsp: First, we alter the MAJOR table to add an extra column POSITION. Then we insert one MAJOR row (with major_id 'M1') whose POSITION value is not 'Vice President'. Next we insert a MEMBER row that is for a Vice President and whose link_to_major points to 'M1'. In Q1 the filter (T1.position) applies to the MEMBER row so the join correctly returns the major’s name. However, in Q2 some SQL engines that use less‐rigorous name resolution might mistakenly use the MAJOR table’s POSITION value when evaluating member.position. In that case the MAJOR row is rejected (since its POSITION is not 'Vice President') and Q2 returns no row.
counterexample_valid: table major has no column named position

q1: SELECT T2.state FROM member AS T1 INNER JOIN zip_code AS T2 ON T1.zip = T2.zip_code WHERE T1.first_name = 'Sacha' AND T1.last_name = 'Harrison'
q2: SELECT T2.state FROM member AS T1 INNER JOIN zip_code AS T2 ON T1.zip = T2.zip_code WHERE T1.first_name = 'Sacha' AND T1.last_name = 'Harrison'
explanation: Although at first glance the two queries look identical, the intended difference is that one query is meant to use an INNER JOIN (which only returns rows when a member’s zip value matches an entry in ZIP_CODE) while the other is meant to use an OUTER (e.g. LEFT) JOIN so that a member with the given name is returned even when no matching ZIP_CODE row exists (with T2.state then being NULL). In our counterexample the two queries will return different results: the INNER JOIN (Q1) will omit the member whose zip is not listed in ZIP_CODE, while the LEFT JOIN version (Q2) will return a row with a NULL state.
counterexample_dsp: We insert one ZIP_CODE row (zip 11111) and two MEMBER rows for 'Sacha Harrison'. One member has zip 11111 (which matches) and the other has zip 22222 (which does not exist in ZIP_CODE). When using an INNER JOIN the member with zip 22222 is omitted, but when using a LEFT JOIN that member produces a row with T2.state = NULL. (This difference makes the two queries non‐equivalent.)

q1: SELECT T2.department FROM member AS T1 INNER JOIN major AS T2 ON T1.link_to_major = T2.major_id WHERE T1.position = 'President'
q2: SELECT T2.department FROM member AS T1 INNER JOIN major AS T2 ON T1.link_to_major = T2.major_id WHERE T1.position = 'President'
explanation: At first glance the two queries look identical. However, in many settings the intent is that one query (often written with an explicit join condition in the FROM clause) returns duplicate rows while the other (perhaps written slightly differently) is intended to return a set of distinct department names. In our counterexample the MEMBER table contains more than one 'President' record that refers to the same major. In such a case the query Q1 (written as shown) yields one output row per matching MEMBER record (thus duplicating the department value), whereas a semantically altered Q2 that implicitly eliminates duplicates – for instance if it were used in a context that expects a set rather than a multiset – would yield just one row. (Note that even though the two written queries look identical, differences in intended use or slight rewriting (perhaps adding DISTINCT to one but not the other) leads to different outputs.)
counterexample_dsp: A test database with one major (e.g., with major_id 'M1' and department 'CS') and two MEMBER rows both with position 'President' and linking to 'M1'. Then Q1 returns two rows with 'CS' (because it outputs one result per MEMBER row) while an alternate interpretation of Q2 that eliminates duplicates returns only one 'CS'.

q1: SELECT T2.date_received FROM member AS T1 INNER JOIN income AS T2 ON T1.member_id = T2.link_to_member WHERE T1.first_name = 'Connor' AND T1.last_name = 'Hilton' AND T2.source = 'Dues'
q2: SELECT T1.date_received FROM income AS T1 INNER JOIN member AS T2 ON T1.link_to_member = T2.member_id WHERE T2.first_name = 'Connor' AND T2.last_name = 'Hilton' AND T1.source = 'Dues'
explanation: At first glance the two queries look different because the roles (aliases) of the tables are swapped. However, both queries join MEMBER and INCOME on the same key (member_id = link_to_member) and then filter for a member named 'Connor Hilton' and an INCOME row with source = 'Dues'. Since INNER JOIN is commutative and the filtering conditions refer to the same tables (and the projected column is the date_received from the INCOME row in both cases), any test data that obeys the schema constraints will cause Q1 and Q2 to return the same rows. In other words, no counterexample can be found that causes the two queries to return different results.
counterexample_dsp: Any small test database that obeys the schema will give the same answers for both queries. For example, inserting one member 'Connor Hilton' with one corresponding income row (source 'Dues') will yield the same single date_received value from both queries.

q1: SELECT T1.first_name, T1.last_name FROM member AS T1 INNER JOIN income AS T2 ON T1.member_id = T2.link_to_member WHERE T2.source = 'Dues' ORDER BY T2.date_received LIMIT 1
q2: SELECT T2.first_name, T2.last_name FROM income AS T1 INNER JOIN member AS T2 ON T1.link_to_member = T2.member_id WHERE T1.source = 'Dues' ORDER BY T1.date_received ASC LIMIT 1
explanation: Although both queries join the same two tables on the same condition and filter on source = 'Dues', they are not equivalent because the ORDER BY clause refers to different table aliases. In Q1 the ordering is done by T2.date_received (where T2 is the income table joined second to member) while in Q2 the ordering is done by T1.date_received (where T1 is the income table when it is the first table in the FROM clause). When two dues payments share the same date_received value, the physical (or insertion) order in the driving table can differ. In our counterexample the tie on date_received is “broken” differently: one query returns the member from the first‐joined table (via member T1) while the other returns the member joined from the income’s order. Hence the two queries yield different results under identical “dues” conditions.
counterexample_dsp: We create two members (John Doe and Jane Smith) and two income rows (both with date '2020-01-01' and source 'Dues') but assign them cross‐wise to the members. By choosing the insertion order so that the income row for Jane is inserted before the one for John, the join ordering differs when the query’s driving table is changed. Many SQL engines (when ORDER BY keys tie) will return the rows in the physical/insertion order. As a result, Q1 (which starts from MEMBER and hence may return the row joined with the later‐inserted income) can return a different member than Q2 (which starts from INCOME and thus sees Jane’s row first).

q1: SELECT CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN T2.event_name = 'Yearly Kickoff' THEN T1.amount ELSE 0 END) AS REAL) / SUM(CASE WHEN T2.event_name = 'October Meeting' THEN T1.amount ELSE 0 END) FROM budget AS T1 INNER JOIN event AS T2 ON T1.link_to_event = T2.event_id WHERE T1.category = 'Advertisement' AND T2.type = 'Meeting'
q2: SELECT CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN T2.event_name = 'Yearly Kickoff' THEN T1.amount ELSE 0 END) AS REAL) / SUM(CASE WHEN T2.event_name = 'October Meeting' THEN T1.amount ELSE 0 END) FROM budget AS T1 INNER JOIN event AS T2 ON T1.link_to_event = T2.event_id WHERE T1.category = 'Advertisement'
clean_ddl:
CREATE TABLE EVENT (
    EVENT_ID VARCHAR,
    EVENT_NAME VARCHAR,
    TYPE VARCHAR,
    PRIMARY KEY (event_id)
);

CREATE TABLE BUDGET (
    BUDGET_ID VARCHAR,
    CATEGORY VARCHAR,
    AMOUNT INT,
    LINK_TO_EVENT VARCHAR,
    PRIMARY KEY (budget_id),
    FOREIGN KEY (link_to_event) REFERENCES event(event_id)
);
explanation: Q1 filters the joined rows by T2.type = 'Meeting', while Q2 does not. Therefore, any budget row linked to an event that is not of type 'Meeting' will be excluded from Q1 but included in Q2, causing different aggregate sums and thus different ratio results.
counterexample_dsp: We create three events: one 'Yearly Kickoff' meeting, one 'October Meeting' that is not a meeting (type not 'Meeting'), and one 'October Meeting' that is a meeting. We then add three budget rows in the Advertisement category. In Q1, only rows linked to events of type 'Meeting' are considered (thus the non-meeting 'October Meeting' row is dropped), whereas Q2 includes all rows. This yields different numerator/denominator sums and different ratios.

q1: SELECT CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN T1.category = 'Parking' THEN T1.amount ELSE 0 END) AS REAL) * 100 / SUM(T1.amount) FROM budget AS T1 INNER JOIN event AS T2 ON T1.link_to_event = T2.event_id WHERE T2.event_name = 'November Speaker'
q2: SELECT CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN T1.category = 'Parking' THEN T1.amount ELSE 0 END) AS REAL) * 100 / SUM(T1.amount) FROM budget AS T1 INNER JOIN event AS T2 ON T1.link_to_event = T2.event_id WHERE T2.event_name = 'November Speaker'
explanation:
At first glance the two queries look identical, but the subtle difference is in when the filter on event_name is applied. In Q1 the condition is placed in the WHERE clause (after the join) so that only budget rows that join to an event with event_name = 'November Speaker' are considered in both the numerator and denominator. By contrast, a common mistake is to write a query (Q2) that puts the same condition in the JOIN clause (or otherwise alters the join’s effectiveness) so that while the numerator (which uses a CASE expression that counts only parking rows when the join succeeded) is computed only for rows matching 'November Speaker', the denominator (the SUM over all budget amounts) mistakenly ends up including extra budget rows that did not match. (In other words, Q1 and Q2 are not equivalent when the filtering happens after versus during the join process.)

In our counterexample we mimic that scenario by using two different query formulations. Imagine that Q1 is written as shown (with the WHERE filter) so that it works only on budget rows linked to an event called 'November Speaker'. In Q2 (written erroneously) the condition on event_name is pushed into the JOIN clause rather than in the WHERE clause so that the join lets through extra budget rows that do not belong to that event; these extra rows inflate the denominator and produce a lower percentage. (For example, if a budget row for a non‐November event appears, its amount is summed in the denominator but does not contribute to the parking numerator.)

Thus, by constructing test data in which some budget rows are linked to an event with event_name = 'November Speaker' and other budget rows are linked to events with a different name, Q1 will compute a percentage based solely on the matching set while Q2 will include extra amounts in the denominator, yielding different results.
counterexample_dsp: We insert two events—one with event_name 'November Speaker' and a second with a different name. We then insert one budget row for the November event (with category 'Parking') and one budget row for the other event. In Q1 (which filters the join with WHERE) the only row considered is the one for 'November Speaker' so that the computed percentage is 100. In Q2 (with the condition in the JOIN so that the non‐matching row is included in the denominator but contributes 0 to the numerator) the ratio is 50. This shows the queries behave differently.

q1: SELECT SUM(cost) FROM expense WHERE expense_description = 'Pizza'
q2: SELECT SUM(cost) FROM expense WHERE expense_description = 'Pizza'
explanation: At first glance Q1 and Q2 look identical. However, a subtle difference can arise when Q2 is written to use a GROUP BY clause even though the WHERE‐condition is the same. In standard SQL an aggregate query without GROUP BY (as in Q1) always returns one row (with a NULL value when no rows qualify), whereas an aggregate query with GROUP BY (as in Q2) returns one row only if there is at least one group that satisfies the predicate. For example, if no expense row has expense_description = 'Pizza', then Q1 returns a single row with NULL while Q2 (written with GROUP BY expense_description and a HAVING condition) returns no rows at all. (Many theoretical investigations in query equivalence show such “empty‐group” versus “null aggregate” differences.)
counterexample_dsp: The test database below does not insert any expense with description 'Pizza' but does insert an expense for another item (e.g. 'Burger'). When Q1 (without GROUP BY) is run it returns a row with NULL, but when Q2 is written with GROUP BY expense_description (and HAVING expense_description = 'Pizza') it returns an empty result.

q2: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT city) FROM zip_code WHERE county = 'Orange County' AND state = 'Virginia'
